cases.n: Juan Orlando Hernández — President 2014–2022
cases.d: Convicted in the Southern District of New York of conspiracy to import cocaine and related weapons counts, and sentenced to 45 years in June 2024. His brother, a former congressman, was convicted in the same district in 2018. He was granted a full and unconditional US presidential pardon on 1 December 2025 and released the same day; Honduras then asked Interpol to execute a 2023 domestic arrest order written to take effect if US authorities freed him. The conviction stands and the sentence goes unserved.
cases.cite: US v. Hernandez, S.D.N.Y., verdict March 2024, sentence June 2024; presidential pardon 1 December 2025; Honduran Ministerio Publico arrest order, December 2025
cases.undone: Pardoned by the US president in December 2025; released the same day.

cases.n: Genaro Garcia Luna — Secretary of Public Security 2006–2012
cases.d: The cabinet minister who ran Mexico’s federal police during the militarised phase of the drug war was convicted in the Eastern District of New York on all five counts, including continuing criminal enterprise, of taking Sinaloa Cartel payments in exchange for protection from arrest, safe passage for shipments and warnings of coming operations. He was sentenced in 2024. In May 2025 a US court ordered him and his wife to pay Mexico more than .4 billion in a civil suit over public contracts, which is the largest financial judgment attached to any official on this map.
cases.cite: US v. Garcia Luna, E.D.N.Y., verdict February 2023, sentence 2024; US civil judgment for the Government of Mexico, May 2025

cases.n: Manuel Noriega — head of state 1983–1989
cases.d: Convicted in Miami federal court of drug trafficking, racketeering and money laundering after the US invasion removed him. The earliest case in which a sitting head of state's control of the security apparatus was prosecuted as a trafficking enterprise.
cases.cite: US v. Noriega, S.D. Fla., 1992

cases.n: Desi Bouterse — head of state, later President
cases.d: Convicted in absentia by a Dutch court in 1999 of trafficking almost 500 kilograms of cocaine and sentenced to eleven years; with no extradition treaty the sentence was never executed and he was subsequently elected president twice. A separate 16-year Surinamese prosecution over the 1982 killing of fifteen political opponents produced a 20-year sentence upheld finally in December 2023. He did not surrender, vanished in January 2024, and died in hiding in December 2024 having served no time on either conviction.
cases.cite: Court of The Hague, cocaine conviction in absentia July 1999; Court of Justice of Suriname, December Murders verdict upheld 20 December 2023; death reported December 2024

cases.n: Jose Americo Bubo Na Tchuto — Navy chief of staff
cases.d: The head of the navy was taken in a DEA sting in international waters and pleaded guilty in New York to conspiring to import cocaine into the United States. The country's air force chief was indicted in the same operation.
cases.cite: US v. Na Tchuto, S.D.N.Y., plea 2014

cases.n: Parapolitica — the Congress investigations
cases.d: Roughly 30% of the Congress was investigated, charged or convicted over collusion with the AUC paramilitaries, who were themselves among the country's largest cocaine traffickers. By April 2012, 139 members of Congress were under investigation; five governors and 32 legislators had been convicted. A later Inspector General review counted more than 500 elected officials investigated over a decade.
cases.cite: Supreme Court of Justice proceedings from 2006; Human Rights Watch; Procuraduria General

cases.n: Vladimiro Montesinos — intelligence chief
cases.d: Head of the national intelligence service under Fujimori and, in practice, of the military, the courts and much of the press. He was convicted on a long series of counts including drug trafficking, and separately sentenced to twenty years for arranging an airdrop of ten thousand assault rifles to Colombian guerrillas. He was accused of sixty-three offences in all and pleaded guilty in 2024 to homicide and forced disappearance in the 1992 killing of six farmers. He videotaped himself paying bribes, which is how much of the record exists: the agency nominally responsible for counter-narcotics kept its own evidence.
cases.cite: Peruvian Supreme Court convictions from 2006; arms-trafficking verdict September 2006; guilty plea, January 2024

cases.n: Rene Sanabria — head of the anti-drug police
cases.d: The former commander of the FELCN, the national anti-narcotics force, and since 2009 head of an elite drug intelligence unit inside the Interior Ministry, was taken in a DEA sting: his group agreed to protect Miami-bound cocaine loads for a 50,000 payment, and one container shipment was seized on arrival. He pleaded guilty in Miami and was sentenced in September 2011 to 14 years, his co-defendant to nine.
cases.cite: US v. Sanabria-Oropeza and Foronda-Azero, S.D. Fla., pleas June 2011, sentences 23 September 2011

cases.n: Edgar Veytia — Attorney General of Nayarit
cases.d: The chief prosecutor of a Mexican state pleaded guilty in Brooklyn to a conspiracy to import heroin, cocaine, methamphetamine and marijuana, and was sentenced in September 2019 to 20 years with  million in forfeiture. Prosecutors established that between 2013 and 2017 he used the office for the H-2 cartel: directing officers to wiretap and arrest rival traffickers, releasing the cartel’s members from custody, and assisting acts of violence. He had campaigned on the claim that there was no room for organised crime in Nayarit. His governor, Roberto Sandoval, was designated by Treasury two months earlier.
cases.cite: US v. Veytia Cambero, E.D.N.Y., guilty plea 2019, sentence 26 September 2019 before Judge Carol Bagley Amon

cases.n: Tomas Yarrington — Governor of Tamaulipas
cases.d: Governor of Tamaulipas from 1999 to 2005 and a presidential candidate, he fled Mexico in 2012, was arrested in Italy in 2017 and extradited the following year. He pleaded guilty in 2021 to conspiring to launder monetary instruments and was sentenced in March 2023 to nine years, having admitted taking more than .5 million in bribes; prosecutors put the laundered total at between .5 and .5 million over fourteen years. The charges that described the trade itself — conspiracy to import cocaine and marijuana, bank fraud — were dismissed under the plea. He was released in November 2024 after a sentence adjustment for time served and returned to Mexico in April 2025 to face a second laundering case.
cases.cite: US v. Yarrington Ruvalcaba, S.D. Tex., plea 25 March 2021, sentence 15 March 2023; Bureau of Prisons release records, 2024; Fiscalia General de la Republica proceedings, 2025

cases.n: Cartel de los Soles indictment
cases.rank: head of state and general staff
cases.d: The US Department of Justice indicted Nicolas Maduro and more than a dozen serving and former officials, including senior military commanders, on narco-terrorism and cocaine importation charges in 2020. Treasury designated the group as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist in July 2025 and the State Department as a Foreign Terrorist Organization from 24 November 2025, saying the regime had corrupted parts of the military, intelligence apparatus, legislature and judiciary to serve it. That designation underpinned a maritime campaign in the Caribbean and Pacific and Maduro was taken into custody on 3 January 2026. Analysts and former officials dispute that it is a formally organised cartel or that he leads one, while agreeing there is government involvement in the trade; the charges have not been tried.
cases.cite: US v. Maduro Moros et al., S.D.N.Y., indictment March 2020; OFAC SDGT designation July 2025; State Department FTO designation effective 24 November 2025; capture reported 3 January 2026

cases.n: Metastasis — judges, prosecutors and police
cases.d: Decryption of a trafficker’s phone produced charges against judges, prosecutors, police commanders and prison officials over case-fixing and protection, the broadest judicial-capture case in the country’s history. After 28 days of hearings the National Court sentenced 20 of 21 defendants in November 2024 to between three and ten years, with public service treated as an aggravating factor. The former president of the Judiciary Council drew nine years and four months for delaying a habeas corpus in favour of a trafficker’s brother for money; another judge was convicted over a release order priced at 00,000. The court sent its ruling back to prosecutors to investigate judges, prosecutors, journalists and lawyers named at trial but never charged. Two fugitives, a former legislator and a businessman, are the subject of extradition requests to Venezuela and the United States.
cases.cite: Fiscalia General del Estado, Caso Metastasis, from December 2023; Corte Nacional de Justicia verdicts, 25 November 2024; extradition requests, 2026

cases.n: Saimir Tahiri — Interior Minister
cases.d: The former interior minister was prosecuted over links to a cannabis-trafficking network and convicted of abuse of office; the trafficking counts did not result in conviction. The case is the clearest test of ministerial-level capture inside an EU candidate state.
cases.cite: Tirana courts, conviction 2019, upheld on appeal

cases.n: Ousmane Conte — son of the head of state
cases.d: Arrested in February 2009 by the junta that took power after the death of his father, the head of state, and charged with trafficking. He confessed on state television to involvement in the cocaine trade; it was not clear whether the confession was coerced. Treasury designated him a kingpin in 2010 while he was held in a Conakry prison and standing trial. No verdict from a competent court followed, which is the pattern across the West African corridor: the admission exists, the judgment does not.
cases.cite: Guinean state television broadcast, February 2009; OFAC Kingpin Act designation, 2010

cases.n: 'Ndrangheta and local administration — Calabria
cases.d: The Rinascita-Scott proceedings convicted officials, lawyers and elected representatives alongside clan members. The organisation is assessed by European law enforcement as controlling a large share of cocaine entering Europe, and dozens of Calabrian municipal councils have been dissolved for mafia infiltration under Italian law.
cases.cite: Tribunale di Vibo Valentia / Catanzaro, Rinascita-Scott verdicts from 2021

cases.n: Port of Antwerp — customs, police and port workers
cases.d: Successive prosecutions have convicted port workers, police officers and customs staff for extracting containers and passing information, in the port through which the largest cocaine volumes in Europe move. In 2022 the Belgian justice minister was placed under protection after a kidnap plot.
cases.cite: Antwerp criminal court proceedings, multiple, 2018–2024

cases.n: Marengo — police and judicial leaks
cases.d: During the Marengo trial a lawyer and a police employee were among those prosecuted for passing protected information to a trafficking network; a witness's lawyer and brother were murdered during the proceedings.
cases.cite: Amsterdam District Court, Marengo proceedings, 2018–2024

cases.n: Captagon production and the state
cases.d: The United States enacted the Captagon Act directing an interagency strategy against production assessed as linked to the Syrian government and associated networks; the UK and EU imposed sanctions on named figures. The assessments are governmental rather than judicial.
cases.cite: Captagon Act (US, 2022); UK and EU sanctions designations, 2023

cases.n: Kamchybek Kolbayev — designated kingpin with state protection
cases.d: Designated under the US Kingpin Act, repeatedly released or lightly sentenced by domestic courts, and killed in a security operation in 2023. The record of releases is the documentary trace of protection.
cases.cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, 2011; Kyrgyz court records

cases.n: Provincial power and the opium economy
cases.d: Successive US government and UN assessments described provincial officials and police commanders taxing and protecting opium production. Very little of it reached a courtroom, which is itself the finding.
cases.cite: UNODC Afghanistan Opium Surveys; US SIGAR reporting

cases.n: Border militias inside the state structure — Shan State
cases.d: Armed groups formally incorporated into the state as border guard forces operate in the areas producing the largest volumes of methamphetamine assessed anywhere. Myanmar scores 10 out of 10 on the synthetic drug indicator and 9 on state-embedded actors.
cases.cite: UNODC Synthetic Drugs in East and Southeast Asia; GI-TOC country profile

cases.n: Municipal police forces disbanded for cartel control
cases.d: Whole municipal forces in Michoacan, Guerrero, Tamaulipas and elsewhere have been disarmed, disbanded or federalised after being assessed as working for trafficking groups. The remedy is administrative, so almost none of it produces a conviction record.
cases.cite: Mexican federal and state government disbandment orders, various

cases.n: Juan Antonio 'Tony' Hernandez — member of Congress
cases.d: The president's brother was convicted in Manhattan of importing cocaine, weapons offences and false statements, and sentenced to life plus 30 years. Trial evidence included cocaine packages stamped TH and testimony that the proceeds funded the National Party's campaigns.
cases.cite: US v. Juan Antonio Hernandez Alvarado, S.D.N.Y., verdict October 2019, sentence March 2021

cases.n: Juan Carlos 'El Tigre' Bonilla — national police chief 2012–2013
cases.d: Extradited in 2022, he pleaded guilty in February 2024 to a cocaine trafficking conspiracy and was sentenced to 19 years. Prosecutors said he took payments to provide armed protection for loads crossing the country; he maintains through his family that the plea was tactical.
cases.cite: US v. Bonilla Valladares, S.D.N.Y., plea February 2024, sentence August 2024

cases.n: Fabio Lobo — son of President Porfirio Lobo
cases.d: Arrested in Haiti in a DEA sting, he pleaded guilty in New York to conspiring to import cocaine and was sentenced to 24 years. He had arranged police escorts for shipments he believed belonged to the Cachiros.
cases.cite: US v. Fabio Porfirio Lobo, S.D.N.Y., plea 2016, sentence September 2017

cases.n: Rosenthal family and Grupo Continental
cases.d: A former vice-president, his son — a congressman and later presidential candidate — and a nephew were designated by OFAC as launderers for the Cachiros; the family's bank was liquidated by Honduran regulators within weeks. Yani Rosenthal pleaded guilty in New York in 2017 and served three years.
cases.cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, October 2015; US v. Yankel Rosenthal, S.D.N.Y., plea 2017

cases.n: Mario Villanueva Madrid — Governor of Quintana Roo 1993–1999
cases.d: Convicted in Mexico and then extradited, he pleaded guilty in Manhattan to laundering proceeds of the Juarez Cartel, which had used the state's coast and airstrips with his protection. He served US and Mexican sentences consecutively across two decades.
cases.cite: US v. Villanueva Madrid, S.D.N.Y., plea 2010, sentence 2011

cases.n: Ivan Reyes Arzate — commander, Federal Police Sensitive Investigative Unit
cases.d: The officer who ran the unit vetted by US agencies for shared intelligence took a $290,000 payment in 2016 to tell the El Seguimiento 39 cartel what that joint investigation knew. He pleaded guilty in Brooklyn and was sentenced to ten years.
cases.cite: US v. Reyes Arzate, E.D.N.Y., plea October 2021, sentence February 2022

cases.n: Salvador Cienfuegos — Secretary of National Defence 2012–2018
cases.d: Arrested in Los Angeles in October 2020 on trafficking and laundering charges, he was released a month later when the Department of Justice dismissed the case at the request of the State Department after Mexico threatened its security cooperation. Mexico's own inquiry closed in 2021 without charges.
cases.cite: US v. Cienfuegos Zepeda, E.D.N.Y., indictment 2019, dismissal November 2020; FGR statement January 2021
cases.undone: Charges dismissed by the Department of Justice at the State Department’s request after Mexico threatened security cooperation.

cases.n: Adan Castillo — director of the anti-narcotics police (SAIA)
cases.d: The head of Guatemala's lead anti-drug agency and his deputy operations chief were arrested during a US-funded training visit to Virginia and pleaded guilty in Washington to conspiring to distribute cocaine bound for the United States.
cases.cite: US v. Castillo Aguilar and Aguilar Garcia, D.D.C., pleas September 2006

cases.n: Roxana Baldetti and Mauricio Lopez Bonilla — Vice-President and Interior Minister
cases.d: Both were indicted in Washington in 2016 on a single count of conspiring to distribute cocaine knowing it would be imported to the United States, over conduct alleged between 2010 and 2015. She denies it. The drug charge has never been tried: a Guatemalan court approved extradition only after her domestic cases are resolved, and those have taken her instead through separate corruption convictions — 15 and a half years in 2018 over a lake-cleaning contract whose chemical proved to be water, salt and chlorine, and 16 years in 2022 for customs fraud. She has been in Guatemalan custody throughout on charges other than the one on this map.
cases.cite: US District Court for the District of Columbia, indictment 2016; Guatemalan convictions October 2018 and 2022; extradition approved subject to prior resolution of domestic cases

cases.n: Romeo Ramos Cruz — mayor of Santa Lucia, Escuintla
cases.d: Extradited in August 2025, the mayor of Santa Lucia in Escuintla pleaded guilty to conspiring to import cocaine. From 2022 to 2024 he used the office to coordinate logistics for a trafficking organisation: in one instance agreeing to disguise a shipment from Venezuela as a delivery of cement, and preparing a letter on official municipal letterhead to help it evade inspection. He faces a maximum of life.
cases.cite: US Department of Justice, District of Columbia, extradition August 2025, guilty plea July 2026

cases.n: Freddy Salazar Flores — Central American Parliament deputy
cases.d: A sitting PARLACEN representative and his father-in-law, named by prosecutors as leaders of the Huistas organisation on the Mexican border, appeared in a Washington court in May 2025 on a 2017 indictment charging cocaine importation. Neither has been tried.
cases.cite: US Department of Justice, District of Columbia, indictment 2017, initial appearances May 2025

cases.n: Prison and social-fabric officials — the gang negotiations
cases.d: The US Treasury designated the director of prisons and the head of the Social Fabric Reconstruction Unit for negotiating with MS-13 and Barrio 18 leaders — privileges and money inside the prisons in exchange for lower homicide figures and electoral support. The government denies the finding, and no case has been tried.
cases.cite: OFAC designations, December 2021; El Faro reporting from 2020

cases.n: General Mauricio Santoyo — presidential security chief
cases.d: The national police general who ran security for President Uribe pleaded guilty in Virginia to providing material support to the AUC, then among Colombia's largest cocaine exporters, and was sentenced to 13 years.
cases.cite: US v. Santoyo Velasco, E.D. Va., plea August 2012

cases.n: Hugo Carvajal — director of military intelligence
cases.d: Extradited from Spain in 2023, he pleaded guilty in June 2025 to cocaine importation, narco-terrorism for the benefit of the FARC and weapons counts. Prosecutors describe him as a leader of the Cartel de los Soles, the network they say runs through the officer corps itself.
cases.cite: US v. Carvajal Barrios, S.D.N.Y., plea June 2025

cases.n: Campo Flores and Flores de Freitas — the first lady's nephews
cases.d: Two nephews of Cilia Flores were arrested in Haiti after offering 800 kilograms of cocaine to DEA informants, convicted in Manhattan and sentenced to 18 years. Both were released to Venezuela in a prisoner exchange in 2022.
cases.cite: US v. Campo Flores and Flores de Freitas, S.D.N.Y., verdict November 2016; prisoner exchange October 2022
cases.undone: Both released to Venezuela in a prisoner exchange in October 2022, six years into 18-year sentences.

cases.n: Maximiliano Davila — director of the anti-narcotics force (FELCN)
cases.d: The head of the FELCN until 2019 was convicted at trial in Manhattan in October 2025 and sentenced to 25 years. Prosecutors showed he steered investigations away from allied traffickers and assigned armed FELCN officers under his command to guard cocaine loads.
cases.cite: US v. Davila Perez, S.D.N.Y., verdict October 2025, sentence March 2026

cases.n: A Ultranza Py — the 2022 network case
cases.d: A cocaine and laundering investigation opened in February 2022 produced charges against police officers, prosecutors and a sitting member of the Chamber of Deputies, and the seizure of hundreds of properties. The central figure fled before arrest and the proceedings continue.
cases.cite: Ministerio Publico del Paraguay, Operativo A Ultranza Py, from February 2022

cases.n: Dino Bouterse — head of the counter-terrorism unit, son of the President
cases.rank: security unit chief and presidential family
cases.d: While running Suriname's counter-terrorism unit he was lured to Panama, arrested, and pleaded guilty in New York to cocaine importation, weapons offences and offering Hezbollah a base in the country. He was sentenced to 16 years.
cases.cite: US v. Dino Bouterse, S.D.N.Y., plea August 2014, sentence March 2015

cases.n: Guy Philippe — senator-elect and former police commander
cases.d: Seized in Port-au-Prince days after winning a Senate seat, he pleaded guilty in Miami to conspiring to launder drug proceeds and was sentenced to nine years. He was deported to Haiti in 2023 and re-entered politics on arrival.
cases.cite: US v. Guy Philippe, S.D. Fla., plea April 2017; deportation November 2023

cases.n: Tivoli Gardens and the Coke extradition
cases.rank: head of government and security forces
cases.d: The government resisted a US extradition request for Christopher Coke for nine months, retaining a Washington law firm to lobby against it; the incursion that followed killed at least 69 people. Coke pleaded guilty in New York in 2011. The commission of enquiry found the operation unjustified in its conduct, and the prime minister had already resigned over the affair.
cases.cite: US v. Christopher Coke, S.D.N.Y., plea August 2011; West Kingston Commission of Enquiry report, 2016

cases.n: General Arnaldo Ochoa and the Interior Ministry — Case No. 1 of 1989
cases.rank: army general and interior ministry officers
cases.d: A decorated general and a Ministry of the Interior colonel who ran the state's hard-currency operations were court-martialled for trafficking cocaine through Cuban waters and airspace, and executed by firing squad in July 1989. The interior minister was dismissed and jailed in the same purge.
cases.cite: Cuban special military tribunal, Causa No. 1, June–July 1989

cases.n: Air force sergeant on the presidential delegation flight
cases.d: A sergeant travelling with the presidential delegation to the G20 was caught in Seville with 39 kilograms of cocaine in his luggage aboard an air force aircraft. He was convicted by a Brazilian military court and sentenced to over ten years.
cases.cite: Superior Tribunal Militar, conviction 2019; Spanish Guardia Civil seizure, June 2019

cases.n: Hugo Tognoli — chief of the Santa Fe provincial police
cases.d: The officer who had headed the province's drug unit before taking command of its police was convicted of protecting a trafficking network around Rosario and sentenced to six years. The city's homicide rate has since run several times the national figure.
cases.cite: Tribunal Oral Federal de Rosario, conviction 2016

cases.n: Operation Guard Shack — Puerto Rico police
cases.d: Eighty-nine law enforcement officers and 44 others were charged after 125 undercover transactions in which officers guarded cocaine deals for $500 to $4,500 apiece. Around 750 FBI personnel were flown in for the arrests; the Bureau called it the largest police corruption case in its history.
cases.cite: US v. Rivera Guzman et al. and 25 related indictments, D.P.R., October 2010

cases.n: Baltimore Gun Trace Task Force
cases.d: An elite plainclothes squad was convicted of racketeering after robbing residents and dealers, reselling seized narcotics through a bail bondsman, and claiming overtime for hours not worked. Prosecutors and the courts have since reviewed hundreds of cases the unit built.
cases.cite: US v. Gondo et al. and US v. Hersl and Taylor, D. Md., pleas and verdicts 2017–2018

cases.n: Jose Irizarry — DEA special agent
cases.d: An agent assigned to money-laundering operations in Colombia diverted laundered funds to himself and his associates, and was sentenced to 12 years. He had used the agency's own undercover accounts, which is why the losses took years to surface.
cases.cite: US v. Irizarry, M.D. Fla., plea 2020, sentence November 2021

cases.n: Ronald Watts — Chicago police sergeant
cases.d: A sergeant and his tactical team ran a protection racket in a public housing development, taxing dealers and framing those who refused. He pleaded guilty to a federal theft charge; courts have since vacated more than 200 convictions built on his team's word.
cases.cite: US v. Watts, N.D. Ill., plea 2013; Cook County exoneration orders from 2017

cases.n: Cameron Ortis — RCMP intelligence director
cases.d: The civilian head of the RCMP's National Intelligence Coordination Centre was convicted under the Security of Information Act of offering operational material to targets, among them the head of the encrypted-phone firm Phantom Secure. He was sentenced to 14 years.
cases.cite: R v. Ortis, Ontario Superior Court, verdict November 2023, sentence February 2024

cases.n: The Djindjic assassination — the JSO and the Zemun clan
cases.d: The prime minister was shot in 2003 by a serving commander of the interior ministry's special operations unit, which had merged with a Zemun criminal group holding a share of the Balkan heroin trade. Twelve were convicted in 2007; the unit was disbanded.
cases.cite: Special Court for Organised Crime, Belgrade, verdicts May 2007

cases.n: Chief special prosecutor, police command and the Kavac clan
cases.d: Sky ECC transcripts passed to Podgorica by Europol produced charges against the former chief special prosecutor, a former assistant police director and his son, a state security officer, over protection of the Kavac clan's cocaine trade. Separate indictments name a former president of the Supreme Court, two former police directors and the mayor of Budva.
cases.cite: Special State Prosecutor's Office of Montenegro, indictments 2023–2024

cases.n: The Susurluk crash
cases.d: A car crash near Susurluk killed a deputy police chief, a wanted trafficker and hitman carrying a diplomatic passport, and left a member of parliament injured. The parliamentary commission that followed documented the working relationship between the security apparatus and heroin trafficking, and produced almost no convictions.
cases.cite: Turkish Grand National Assembly Susurluk commission report, 1997

cases.n: Moscow drug squad officers — the Golunov case
cases.d: Five officers of a Moscow district drug unit were convicted of planting narcotics on a journalist and sentenced to between five and twelve years. The case is the rare Russian instance where the fabrication of a drug charge by serving officers reached a verdict.
cases.cite: Moscow City Court, verdict 2022

cases.n: The OCRTIS 'coups d'achat' file
cases.d: The former head of the national anti-drug office was placed under formal investigation over cannabis shipments run through an informer, in a case turning on how far a police service may let a trade operate to reach the people behind it. He denies wrongdoing.
cases.cite: French judicial investigation opened 2019, Paris; Cour de cassation rulings on related seizures

cases.n: Operation Venetic — officers among those convicted
cases.d: The EncroChat material produced thousands of UK prosecutions, among them serving police and prison officers who had sold information or moved contraband. The corruption was found by reading the traffickers' messages rather than by internal detection.
cases.cite: National Crime Agency Operation Venetic reporting, from 2020

cases.n: Cai Dongjia — party secretary of Boshe village, Lufeng
cases.d: Three thousand police raided the village in December 2013 and seized three tonnes of methamphetamine; officials put a fifth of its households in the trade and said Boshe had supplied a third of China's meth. The party secretary who had shielded the labs and tipped off suspects was sentenced to death in 2016 and executed in 2019; a Lufeng drug squad captain was detained in the same investigation.
cases.cite: Guangdong Higher People's Court, sentence 2016; Xinhua, execution January 2019

cases.n: The Pong Su — a state-linked vessel
cases.d: A North Korean freighter delivered 125 kilograms of heroin to a beach in Victoria in 2003 and was boarded by Australian special forces. The captain and senior crew were acquitted of importation in 2006 — the jury was not persuaded they knew the cargo — and the ship was later sunk as a bombing target. The state link was never established in court.
cases.cite: R v. Song and others, Supreme Court of Victoria, acquittals March 2006

cases.n: Teddy Minahasa — police inspector general
cases.d: A two-star general days from taking command of the Jakarta police was convicted of ordering seized methamphetamine to be replaced with alum and sold on. Prosecutors sought death; the court imposed life imprisonment, later reduced on appeal.
cases.cite: West Jakarta District Court, verdict May 2023

cases.n: The 'ninja cops' and recycled seizures
cases.d: A Senate inquiry examined officers who reported partial seizures and resold the rest, a practice known locally as ninja cops. The chief of the national police resigned in October 2019 over his handling of a 2013 case in Pampanga; the administrative and criminal proceedings that followed produced no senior conviction.
cases.cite: Philippine Senate Committee on Public Order hearings, 2019; PNP internal affairs records

cases.n: Narcotics Control Bureau — the Mumbai zonal office
cases.d: The CBI registered a case in 2023 against the former zonal director of the Narcotics Control Bureau in Mumbai and three colleagues, alleging a demand for payment to keep a name out of a high-profile cruise-ship seizure file. He denies the allegation and the case has not been tried.
cases.cite: Central Bureau of Investigation FIR, May 2023; Bombay High Court proceedings

cases.n: Abdur Rahman Bodi — member of parliament for Cox's Bazar
cases.d: The MP for the district through which almost all yaba enters Bangladesh appeared on the government's own list of traffickers. He was convicted in 2018 of concealing wealth and jailed for three years; the trafficking allegations themselves were never brought to trial, and 102 dealers, several of them his relatives, surrendered in a staged ceremony in 2019.
cases.cite: Dhaka Special Judge's Court, Anti-Corruption Commission case, conviction February 2018

cases.n: Ahmed Wali Karzai — Kandahar provincial council
cases.rank: provincial council chairman and presidential family
cases.d: The president's half-brother, who chaired the Kandahar provincial council and was reported to be on the CIA payroll, was described by US officials as a participant in the opium trade. He denied it, was never charged in any court, and was shot dead by his own security chief in 2011.
cases.cite: US State Department and military reporting, 2009–2010; SIGAR and UNODC assessments

cases.n: Raiymbek Matraimov — deputy chief of customs
cases.d: Designated by the US Treasury under the Magnitsky Act for a customs scheme that moved hundreds of millions of dollars out of the country. Journalists who documented the network were prosecuted or forced out; he settled a domestic corruption case by repayment and served no prison term at the time.
cases.cite: OFAC Global Magnitsky designation, December 2020; OCCRP and Kloop investigations 2019–2020

cases.n: Captagon on a private jet — the Beirut airport arrest
cases.d: A member of the Saudi royal family and four others were detained at Beirut airport in October 2015 while loading two tonnes of captagon onto a private jet. Lebanese prosecutors charged them; no verdict in the case has been made public.
cases.cite: Lebanese Internal Security Forces statement and public prosecution filing, October 2015

cases.n: The Akasha file — judges, prosecutors and police
cases.d: Two brothers running a Mombasa heroin organisation pleaded guilty in New York, and their obstruction count was an admission that they had paid Kenyan judges, prosecutors and police officers over two years to block their extradition. None of the officials who took the money has been named or charged in Kenya.
cases.cite: US v. Baktash Akasha Abdalla et al., S.D.N.Y., pleas October 2018, sentences 2019

cases.n: Abba Kyari — deputy commissioner of police
cases.d: The head of the police Intelligence Response Team was charged by the drug agency with substituting seized cocaine and offering an officer 1,400 to stop it being tested. In March 2026 a judge acquitted him and two brothers on a separate 23-count asset-declaration charge, describing that prosecution as persecution. The cocaine trial continues before a different judge alongside four suspended officers of his unit; two traffickers originally charged with them pleaded guilty and were jailed. He has been in detention since 2022.
cases.cite: NDLEA charges, Federal High Court Abuja, from February 2022; acquittal on asset-declaration counts, March 2026; substantive drug trial continuing before Justice Nwite

cases.n: Ibraima Papa Camara — air force chief of staff
cases.d: Indicted in New York alongside the navy chief for conspiring to store and move cocaine through the country, and named earlier by the US Treasury as a trafficker. He remained in Bissau and was never surrendered.
cases.cite: US v. Na Tchuto and Camara, S.D.N.Y., indictment 2013; OFAC Kingpin designation 2010

cases.n: The MV Benjamin cocaine and the Boakye tapes
cases.d: Seventy-seven parcels of cocaine landed from a vessel and disappeared; a recording then surfaced of a senior police officer meeting suspects at his home. The committee of enquiry led by a Supreme Court judge found the police account unsatisfactory, and the officer returned to duty.
cases.cite: Georgina Wood Committee report, Government of Ghana, 2006

cases.n: Air Cocaine — the Tarkint airstrip
cases.d: A Boeing 727 that had flown from Venezuela was unloaded at a desert strip and then burned. UN and national investigations pointed to protection by local officials and armed groups; the arrests made in Bamako produced no senior conviction, and the aircraft's owners were never established.
cases.cite: UNODC and UN Panel of Experts reporting from 2010; Malian judicial proceedings

cases.n: Christiaan Prinsloo — police colonel, firearms to the Cape gangs
cases.d: A colonel sold roughly two thousand firearms from police stores to Cape Flats gangs, and was sentenced to 18 years. Ballistics have since linked the guns to more than a thousand shootings, many of them in the drug turf conflicts of the Flats.
cases.cite: Bellville Regional Court, plea and sentence 2016; SAPS ballistics evidence

cases.n: Hernan Bermudez Requena — Secretary of Security of Tabasco
cases.d: The state's top police official from 2018 to 2024 is accused of running La Barredora, a group tied to the CJNG, from the office itself. He fled Mexico in early 2025, was arrested in Paraguay in September and returned within days; he is held at the Altiplano federal prison on criminal association, extortion and kidnapping charges.
cases.cite: Fiscalia General del Estado de Tabasco warrant, February 2025; Paraguayan SENAD arrest and expulsion, September 2025

cases.n: Piedras Negras prison, Coahuila
cases.d: A state prison was used by Los Zetas as a base, workshop and disposal site, with the administration handing over control of parts of the facility. Testimony in Texas trials and a state investigation established the arrangement; the prosecutions that followed reached staff rather than the officials who authorised it.
cases.cite: Coahuila state attorney general investigation, 2016–2017; testimony in US v. Trevino Morales, W.D. Tex.

cases.n: Jose Armando Ubico Aguilar — member of Congress 2016–2024
cases.d: Indicted in Texas in 2021 while sitting in Congress, he pleaded guilty in May 2024 to an international trafficking conspiracy, admitting he passed drug-related information and cash to another Guatemalan official on a trafficker's behalf.
cases.cite: US v. Ubico Aguilar, E.D. Tex., indictment March 2021, plea May 2024

cases.n: Cliver Alcala Cordones — retired army major general
cases.d: Charged in the same 2020 indictment as Maduro, he surrendered to the DEA in Colombia, pleaded guilty to providing material support including firearms to the FARC, and was sentenced to 260 months in April 2024. He is the first of that indictment's defendants to be sentenced.
cases.cite: US v. Alcala Cordones, S.D.N.Y., plea 2023, sentence April 2024

cases.n: Campo de Gibraltar police — the Algeciras cases
cases.d: A municipal officer and two national police officers were sentenced in April 2024 to more than seven years each for guarding a 367-kilogram cocaine load. A separate 2022 operation arrested five municipal officers at the port of Algeciras along with an officer stationed in Ceuta, a customs official and a former police official, over 6.2 tonnes moved through the strait.
cases.cite: Audiencia Provincial de Cadiz, sentence April 2024; Policia Nacional operation, Algeciras, 2022

cases.n: Antwerp police arrests and the Brussels mega-trial
cases.d: Twenty-two people including three serving police officers were arrested in January 2024 over cocaine moving through Antwerp. In October 2024 a Brussels court sentenced dozens in the country's largest trafficking trial, built almost entirely on decrypted Sky ECC and EncroChat traffic; 116 tonnes of cocaine were seized at the port in 2023 alone.
cases.cite: Belgian federal police operation, January 2024; Brussels correctional court verdicts, October 2024

cases.n: Inez Weski — defence counsel in the Marengo case
cases.d: The lawyer for Ridouan Taghi was arrested in April 2023 on suspicion of relaying messages between her client in a maximum-security prison and his organisation, using the privileged channel between counsel and detainee. She had sold her law office to her son and formally retired ten days before the arrest. The Rotterdam District Court convicted her in May 2026 of participating in the organisation, and set the sentence equal to the 42 days she had already spent in pre-trial detention, so she served no further time. Taghi himself was sentenced to life in February 2024.
cases.cite: Rechtbank Rotterdam, conviction May 2026; Openbaar Ministerie arrest April 2023; Taghi life sentence, February 2024

cases.n: Hanoi and Phu Tho narcotics officers
cases.d: Two former officers of a Hanoi district drug investigation team were indicted in 2024 for shielding a Laos–Vietnam network that moved 137 kilograms; a senior officer in Viet Tri was sentenced to life in 2025 for financing a 12,000-tablet purchase he intended to convert into a staged arrest. Vietnam executes traffickers at these weights, which is the measure of what the officers were protecting.
cases.cite: Supreme People's Procuracy indictments, 2024; Hanoi People's Court verdict, 2025

cases.n: Tareck El Aissami — Executive Vice-President
cases.d: Designated under the Kingpin Act weeks after his appointment as vice-president, for facilitating shipments out of Venezuela and protecting traffickers operating inside it. Treasury designated his frontman and a network of petroleum, engineering and holding companies at the same time. The finding is executive, not judicial, and has never been tested at trial.
cases.cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, February 2017

cases.n: Isidro Avelar Gutierrez — federal magistrate judge
cases.d: A sitting federal magistrate was designated under the Kingpin Act for taking payments from the CJNG and Los Cuinis in exchange for favourable rulings for senior members. Judicial capture rarely produces a case in Mexico, and this one arrived as a US sanctions listing rather than a domestic prosecution.
cases.cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, May 2019

cases.n: Roberto Sandoval Castaneda — Governor of Nayarit 2011–2017
cases.d: Designated under the Global Magnitsky order for taking bribes from the CJNG and earlier from the Beltran Leyva organisation in exchange for information and protection, and for misappropriating state assets. His own attorney general, Edgar Veytia, had already pleaded guilty in Brooklyn two months earlier — the state's two senior law-enforcement figures reached the same finding by different routes.
cases.cite: OFAC designation under E.O. 13818, May 2019

cases.n: Erik Suniga Rodriguez — municipal mayor, the Los Pochos organisation
cases.d: A serving mayor was designated as a significant foreign narcotics trafficker along with the organisation named after him, four associates and five Guatemalan companies. Treasury redesignated the group in 2024, noting a change of leadership and its members' continuing involvement in local politics.
cases.cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, December 2019; redesignation under E.O. 14059, February 2024

cases.n: Michel Martelly — President 2011–2016
cases.d: Designated by the US Treasury for trafficking activity, including sponsoring and financing gangs, in a country where the gang system and the cocaine transit route have merged. Canada had sanctioned him earlier over gang financing. He denies the allegations; no court has heard them.
cases.cite: OFAC designation under E.O. 14059, August 2024; Global Affairs Canada sanctions, November 2022

cases.n: Gustavo Petro — sitting President
cases.d: The United States designated the sitting Colombian president under its illicit-drug order in October 2025, citing a rise in coca cultivation under his administration and the handling of intelligence channels. Colombia rejected the finding, and the two governments' assessments of the same period diverge sharply. This is an executive designation rather than a charge, and belongs on the map as one.
cases.cite: OFAC designation under E.O. 14059, October 2025; Government of Colombia response

cases.n: The Assad family and the Fourth Division — the captagon designations
cases.d: Three cousins of the president were designated by the US, UK and EU across March and April 2023 over captagon production and smuggling, alongside the manager of the Fourth Division's revenues and militia leaders in the south. Treasury put one Latakia facility's output at 84 million pills in 2020. The EU stated the trade had become a regime-led business model; the findings are executive and no court has heard them.
cases.cite: OFAC designations under E.O. 13572 and 13582, March 2023; UK FCDO designations, March 2023; Council of the EU designations, April 2023

cases.n: Amer Khiti — member of parliament and captagon logistics
cases.d: A sitting member of the Syrian parliament was designated by the UK and the EU over companies used to produce, package and move captagon. Legislative office in this case is not protection bought from the trade but a position held inside it.
cases.cite: UK FCDO designation, March 2023; Council of the EU designation, April 2023

cases.n: Taliban shadow ministry — the 2012 Kingpin designation
cases.d: A Taliban figure designated under the Kingpin Act in 2012 for his role in narcotics trafficking was, by late 2017, serving as the movement's shadow foreign minister and managing its relations with Iran. He also sits on the UN Security Council's 1988 sanctions list, which is the rare instance of the same person appearing on a drug list and a counter-terrorism list for the same conduct.
cases.cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, November 2012; UN Security Council Resolution 1988 sanctions list

cases.n: Los Cuellos Blancos del Puerto — the Callao judiciary
cases.rank: supreme court judge, court president and judicial council
cases.d: Wiretaps placed on a Callao trafficking organisation caught a different network on the same lines: a supreme court judge, the president of the Callao superior court and members of the judicial appointments council trading sentence reductions, promotions and favours. The judge fled to Spain, the court president was jailed, and the first conviction after a full trial came only in November 2025, seven years on. Several implicated judges were still sitting while under investigation.
cases.cite: IDL-Reporteros audio releases from July 2018; Corte Superior Nacional de Justicia Penal Especializada, first trial verdict November 2025

cases.n: Operacao Tacitus — Sao Paulo civil police and the PCC
cases.d: Prosecutors allege a police chief, an officer and three investigators of the Sao Paulo civil police negotiated around 30 million reais in payments to shield PCC members from investigations, one of them producing a false document for the faction. Authorising the arrests, the judge wrote that no faction reaches the PCC's scale without the participation of public officials in the security services. The defence says the facts were investigated and shelved previously and calls the arrests arbitrary.
cases.cite: Ministerio Publico de Sao Paulo, Operacao Tacitus, arrests December 2024

cases.n: General Dom Hak — military intelligence chief
cases.d: A two-star general was arrested with seven others after police found 35 kilograms of heroin and manufacturing equipment in a Phnom Penh house. The government burned the seizure publicly before prosecutors had begun, then released him within weeks for lack of evidence. It remains the highest-ranking Cambodian drug case to reach a court.
cases.cite: Phnom Penh Municipal Court, charge and release October 2003

cases.n: Mario Ruiz Massieu — Deputy Attorney General 1993–1994
cases.d: The official who ran Mexico's counter-narcotics prosecutions moved about $9 million into Houston bank accounts in cash, carried by an aide on some twenty-five commercial flights. A Houston civil jury found the money was paid by traffickers, principally the Gulf Cartel, for protection. He fought extradition under house arrest for four years and killed himself in New Jersey in 1999 before the criminal case was tried.
cases.cite: US civil forfeiture proceedings, S.D. Tex., jury finding 1997; extradition litigation 1995–1999

cases.n: Proceso 8000 — the Samper campaign accounts
cases.rank: head of state and campaign officials
cases.d: Prosecutors established that the Cali cartel had put money into the 1994 presidential campaign; the campaign treasurer, the defence minister and the comptroller were convicted, and a congressional commission cleared the president himself in a vote his opponents called a whitewash. The United States revoked his visa. It is the earliest case on this map where a national election, rather than an agency, was the thing bought.
cases.cite: Fiscalia General de la Nacion, Proceso 8000, from 1995; Camara de Representantes vote, June 1996

cases.n: General Antonio Indjai — armed forces chief of staff
cases.d: The general who led the 2012 coup was charged in New York with conspiring to distribute cocaine and to arm the FARC, including a proposal to move their cocaine through the country and supply surface-to-air missiles in return. He was never surrendered. With the navy and air force chiefs charged in the same period, the entire senior command stood accused at once.
cases.cite: US v. Indjai, S.D.N.Y., indictment 2013

cases.n: The vanished 975 kilograms
cases.d: The director of the judicial police said 975 of 980 kilograms seized in November 2021 had disappeared from official custody, and that police and security personnel were suspected of taking it. One officer was arrested. The country had not tried a drug case since 2005, which is the context for a seizure evaporating rather than becoming evidence.
cases.cite: Guinea-Bissau Policia Judiciaria statement, February 2022; US Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearing record, 2009

cases.n: The 2008 Lungi cocaine flight
cases.d: A twin-engine aircraft carrying around 700 kilograms of cocaine landed at Lungi airport in July 2008 marked with Red Cross insignia. The prosecutions that followed reached airport and security personnel alongside the foreign crew, and were described in US congressional testimony as historic for the region — the point of comparison being Guinea-Bissau, which had tried no drug case since 2005.
cases.cite: Sierra Leone High Court convictions, 2009; US Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearing, June 2009

cases.n: Operation Black Tie — officials in the Nizic network
cases.d: Twenty-three people were arrested in Sarajevo in April 2024 over trafficking and laundering for the inner circle of a kingpin already sentenced in the Netherlands. Europol stated that those detained included not only accomplices but corrupt officials identified as facilitators of the network. The case is Bosnia's first documented reach into the state layer of a Balkan cocaine organisation.
cases.cite: Europol and Bosnian security agencies, Operation Black Tie, April 2024

cases.n: Upakit Pachariyangkun — senator
cases.d: A sitting senator was indicted on narcotics trafficking and laundering charges tied to a Myanmar businessman arrested in Bangkok in 2022 and sanctioned by the US over support for the junta. His Thai-American son-in-law was among those arrested; the narcotics board seized property worth over 400 million baht from his residences. The case reaches from Shan State production into the Thai upper house.
cases.cite: Thai Office of the Attorney General indictment, 2023; Narcotics Control Board seizures; OFAC designations of the associated network

cases.n: Giulio Andreotti — seven-time Prime Minister
cases.d: Prosecutors charged that he had put the influence of his office at Cosa Nostra's disposal in exchange for electoral support, and that the organisation expected him to fix the Maxi Trial, the case that had convicted 475 of its members for a heroin economy running through New York. He was acquitted in 1999 and again in 2003; the appellate judges found ties to mobsters before 1980 but held the limitation period had expired. The Court of Cassation closed the matter in 2004.
cases.cite: Tribunale di Palermo, acquittal October 1999; Corte d'Appello 2003; Corte di Cassazione 2004

cases.n: Federal judges of Oran and Salta
cases.d: A federal judge in Oran was sentenced to 13 years in 2019 as head of an association that took money and property in exchange for rulings favouring traffickers. The same trafficker had bought a different federal judge in 2007, who was removed and convicted; that magistrate killed himself in 2020 as his arrest approached. A federal judge in Mendoza was separately charged over links to trafficking groups.
cases.cite: Tribunal Oral Federal de Salta, conviction of ex-judge Reynoso, March 2019; earlier conviction of judge Sola Torino, 2007

cases.n: Caso Purga — the Guayas courts
cases.d: A parallel file on judicial corruption in Guayas province charged judges alongside a former legislator described by prosecutors as the power behind the provincial courts. Testimony described payments arranged to obtain releases, including a failed attempt to free a former vice-president. Sentence reductions granted by prison-guarantee judges, outside their competence, were the recurring mechanism.
cases.cite: Ecuadorian Fiscalia General del Estado, Caso Purga, from 2024

cases.n: Judge Amaury de Lima e Souza — criminal enforcement court, Juiz de Fora
cases.d: Federal police arrested the judge of the criminal enforcement court in 2014 during an operation against an international trafficking route running from Bolivia through Paraguay into Minas Gerais and on to Rio and the north-east. Investigators found a series of rulings he had signed for traffickers, one granting house arrest to a defendant the prosecutors had charged. He was sentenced in 2022 to 24 years and four months.
cases.cite: Tribunal de Justica de Minas Gerais, 5th criminal chamber, sentence October 2022; Policia Federal operation, June 2014

cases.n: Cartel de la Toga — the Supreme Court bribery network
cases.rank: supreme court presidents and anti-corruption prosecutor
cases.d: Two former presidents of the Supreme Court, a sitting magistrate and the national anti-corruption prosecutor were convicted of taking payments to shelve or steer criminal proceedings against members of Congress, including men under investigation in the parapolitica files over ties to the AUC. One ex-president drew 16 years; another was sentenced to 10 in February 2026 with an Interpol red notice; the prosecutor was convicted in Colombia and separately in Miami. The bribes bought the appeal layer above the cases this map already records.
cases.cite: Corte Suprema de Justicia de Colombia, Sala Especial, convictions 2021–2026; US v. Moreno Rivera, S.D. Fla., 2019

cases.n: Prosecutor charged over Gulf Clan assets
cases.d: A serving prosecutor was charged with lending her name to conceal property belonging to a front man for the Gulf Clan, the country's largest cocaine trafficking organisation, and placed under house arrest. The mechanism is the quiet one: not a case fixed, but title held.
cases.cite: Fiscalia General de la Nacion charge and house arrest order, July 2023

cases.n: The Michoacanazo — mayors and officials released
cases.d: Federal police arrested more than 30 state and municipal officials, including ten mayors, in May 2009 for alleged ties to La Familia Michoacana. Within two years every one of them had been released, the federal judiciary finding the prosecution's evidence insufficient. The episode set the federal government against the state and against its own courts, and is the clearest instance on this map of a mass capture case collapsing without a single conviction.
cases.cite: Procuraduria General de la Republica prosecutions, May 2009; federal judicial releases 2009-2011; Mexican Law Review study of the case

cases.n: Operation Eureka — 76 convictions
cases.d: A Reggio Calabria bunker court convicted 76 defendants and acquitted seven in October 2025, in a case built from a 2023 carabinieri operation that seized three tonnes of cocaine and arrested 108 people. Prosecutors described three trafficking associations run by the most powerful Ionian 'Ndrangheta families. It is the counterweight to the capture entries: the same state whose Calabrian councils are dissolved for infiltration also runs the courts that convict at this scale.
cases.cite: Tribunale di Reggio Calabria, Operation Eureka first-instance verdicts, October 2025; DDA Reggio Calabria and ROS carabinieri investigation, May 2023

cases.n: Border Guard officers of the Vakhsh checkpoint
cases.rank: border guard officers and provincial police
cases.d: A military court in Khatlon sentenced five Border Guard Service officers to between three and 21 years, the longest for the former chief of the Vakhsh checkpoint on the Afghan frontier, in whose office investigators had found 20 kilograms of hashish. A senior Khatlon police official was arrested the same day with 12 kilograms of heroin. Roughly 90 tonnes of heroin cross Central Asia each year and most seizures are of small dealers; this is the rank at which the record stops.
cases.cite: Khatlon military court, sentences November 2012; State Committee for National Security statement, November 2012

cases.n: The ambassador and the deputy interior minister
cases.d: Tajikistan's ambassador to Kazakhstan was arrested in Almaty in 2000 with 86 kilograms of heroin in his car. The following year the deputy interior minister was murdered, and prosecutors argued at trial that he was killed for refusing to pay for a 50-kilogram consignment. Estimates in 2014 put drug money at up to 30 percent of the country's economy.
cases.cite: Kazakh authorities, arrest in Almaty 2000; Tajik prosecution case in the 2001 killing; UNODC and academic estimates

cases.n: Harun Mwau — legislator and assistant transport minister
cases.d: Designated by the US as a drug kingpin in 2011 while a sitting member of parliament. He had headed the national anti-corruption agency, funded a presidential campaign, and been appointed assistant transport minister with responsibility for container arrangements and the Ports Authority. He resigned after being named in parliament, has consistently denied the allegations, and was absolved by a police investigation researchers described as conducted in controversial circumstances.
cases.cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, June 2011; Kenyan parliamentary naming and subsequent police inquiry

cases.n: Jackie Selebi — national police commissioner and Interpol president
cases.d: The head of the South African police, and simultaneously president of Interpol, was convicted of corruption in 2010 over payments from a drug trafficker and sentenced to 15 years. The wife of the state security minister was convicted separately in 2011 of conspiring to traffic. No other country on this map has convicted a serving Interpol president.
cases.cite: South Gauteng High Court, conviction July 2010, sentence August 2010; Supreme Court of Appeal 2011; separate conviction of Sheryl Cwele, 2011

cases.n: The protected heroin corridor
cases.d: Researchers documented a trafficking system running for three decades with, in their words, a tight integration between ruling party figures and traffickers, and near-zero heroin seizures as the evidence of it. The principal named figure was designated abroad as a trafficker while remaining a prominent businessman at home. Family members were arrested in Portugal and Eswatini and one was shot dead in Maputo in 2012; none was ever charged in Mozambique.
cases.cite: Global Initiative and ENACT research by Haysom, Gastrow and Shaw, 2018; LSE International Development working paper 18-190

cases.n: Police command and airport security — the 2026 charges
cases.d: After the country's largest recorded seizure, close to four tonnes of cocaine bound for Europe, the police inspector general stated that senior government officials were involved in trafficking. The national police charged the head of its Major Crimes Unit and another official, and named a deputy commander responsible for security at Roberts International Airport as an active participant. Twelve suspects were charged in the seizure case; a former vice-president was separately indicted on trafficking counts.
cases.cite: Liberia National Police charges and Inspector General statements, 2026; indictment of the former vice-president, 2026

cases.n: The minister of transport and aviation
cases.d: The minister responsible for transport and aviation was dismissed after proceedings in the Lungi cocaine case indicated he had provided landing clearance for the aircraft carrying around 700 kilograms. The dismissal was administrative; the allegation itself was never tried.
cases.cite: Sierra Leone government dismissal, 2008–2009; Africa Center for Strategic Studies review of the case

cases.n: Operation Relentless — bribing the government that reported it
cases.d: South American and West African traffickers were recorded paying senior Liberian officials to guarantee safe passage and storage for multi-tonne cocaine shipments. The officials reported the approaches and worked with the DEA instead, producing extraditions to New York and convictions there. The DEA called the cooperation from the highest levels of the Liberian government unprecedented, which is the measure of how rare that response is on this map.
cases.cite: US v. Umeh, Salazar Castano, Kamara and others, S.D.N.Y., indictments and convictions from 2010

cases.n: Gamboa Sanchez — Minister of Public Security and judge
cases.rank: vice-minister of public security, later judge
cases.d: A former Vice Minister of Public Security who later sat as a judge, designated by Treasury in August 2025 for facilitating the movement of tens of millions of dollars' worth of cocaine from Colombia through Costa Rica to the United States and Europe. Treasury's finding is what distinguishes him from the other officials here: he used his network of contacts inside the government to obtain information about ongoing counter-narcotics investigations. He was arrested in June 2025 on a US extradition request, weeks after Costa Rica's president signed a constitutional reform permitting the extradition of Costa Rican nationals for drug trafficking and terrorism — a change that made his own removal possible.
cases.cite: US Treasury press release sb0227 and OFAC designation under E.O. 14059, 15 August 2025; Costa Rican arrest, 23 June 2025; constitutional reform on extradition signed May 2025

cases.n: Caso Colorado — police officers on the Caribbean corridor
cases.d: Investigators established regular telephone contact between an organisation holding the Caribbean lowland corridor and officers stationed at Guapiles and Cariari de Pococi. Some were recruited specifically to warn of raids, checkpoints and investigator movements in time for drugs to be moved or hidden. Five officers were charged before the specialised organised crime court.
cases.cite: Organismo de Investigacion Judicial, case file 21-000115-0622-PE; Fiscalia Adjunta contra el Narcotrafico charges, 2026

cases.n: The DNCD and the armed forces
cases.d: Three senior officials of the National Drug Control Agency were arrested providing security to traffickers awaiting a shipment bound for Puerto Rico. A navy officer responsible for port security was accused of moving 800 kilograms to Spain; nearly twenty officials, mostly navy, were accused in 2008 of killing seven Colombian traffickers to take 1.3 tonnes. Since 2009 more than 700 DNCD personnel have been removed, around 200 of them suspected of trafficking, and the national police expelled about 1,400 officers from 2010.
cases.cite: DNCD arrests and dismissal statistics reported 2012-2013; Dominican prosecutions of navy and police personnel

cases.n: The Escobar of the Sahara trial — legislators and a regional council president
cases.d: A Casablanca court sentenced 29 people in June 2026 after a two-year trial, among them a construction figure and former head of a regional council who drew 12 years, and two former members of parliament from the governing party who drew 10 each. The case began with testimony from a jailed Malian trafficker who said his Moroccan political associates had seized his assets after his 2019 arrest, and covered tonnes of cannabis resin moved across North Africa alongside Latin American cocaine. Charges included drug and gold trafficking, corruption and laundering; one defendant was acquitted and appeals are open.
cases.cite: Casablanca Court of Appeal, verdicts 26 June 2026

cases.n: Serving and former police officers — the 2025 designations
cases.d: Two Guyanese law enforcement officers were designated on 5 June 2025: one serving, for arranging safe passage for Mexican and Venezuelan traffickers moving cocaine through the country, and one former officer wanted over the abduction of a policeman in 2024. Neither has been tried. Treasury noted that Guyana is a close US partner and that the State Department nonetheless treats corruption there as a significant obstacle to its own counter-narcotics effort — an ally and a problem named in the same paragraph. The network they served is recorded separately on the company layer.
cases.cite: US Treasury press release sb0156 and OFAC designations under E.O. 14059, 5 June 2025; ICE HSI New York investigation

cases.n: The Phantom Squad
cases.d: Guyana's most powerful trafficker ran an armed group that operated alongside the state during a period of killings in the mid-2000s, using construction and forestry businesses to launder cocaine proceeds moved from Colombia to the United States. He was convicted in New York and served 15 years. The squad's relationship to the government was examined publicly and never resolved in a Guyanese court.
cases.cite: US v. Khan, E.D.N.Y., conviction and 15-year sentence; Guyanese public inquiries into the killings of 2002-2006

cases.n: The Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone
cases.d: The government granted a Chinese company a concession in the Lao section of the Golden Triangle in 2007. Treasury later designated its head and his wife over heroin and methamphetamine trafficking and laundering. The US State Department reported that the zone is controlled and administered in part by transnational criminal organisations, that jurisdictional confusion between officials and zone security hinders investigation, and that no complicit official has been investigated, prosecuted or convicted. Laos arrested more than 20,000 people for drug offences between 2015 and 2019.
cases.cite: OFAC Transnational Criminal Organizations designation, January 2018; US State Department Trafficking in Persons Report 2024

cases.n: 'Criminals in uniform' — the constabulary and the black flights
cases.d: After a Cessna loaded with 548 kilograms of cocaine crashed on a makeshift runway outside Port Moresby, the police commissioner said publicly that there are criminals in uniform in the constabulary and committed to removing them. The Australian-based organisers were convicted in Victoria and the pilot drew 18 years in a PNG jail; the officers alleged to have enabled the night flights were not charged. Fiji's drug intelligence chief has raised the same concern about infiltration of law enforcement there.
cases.cite: Royal Papua New Guinea Constabulary statements, 2020; Victoria County Court sentences, July 2026; Lowy Institute analysis of Pacific trafficking

cases.n: Ruben Rocha Moya — sitting Governor of Sinaloa
cases.d: A sitting governor and nine other current and former Sinaloa officials, among them a senator, a state deputy attorney general, a former public security secretary, police commanders and the mayor of Culiacan, were indicted in Manhattan in April 2026 over a protection arrangement with the Chapitos faction. Prosecutors allege he met the faction before the 2021 election and undertook to install friendly officials, that cartel members stole ballot boxes and intimidated rivals to secure his victory, and that he then let them consolidate control of state and local law enforcement. He rejects the accusations. Mexico said the extradition request lacked sufficient evidence and opened its own inquiry; none of the ten is in custody. He announced his resignation on 1 May 2026, days after the indictment, calling it a political attack; the mayor of Culiacan stepped down in the same week.
cases.cite: US v. Rocha Moya et al., S.D.N.Y., indictment unsealed 29 April 2026; Fiscalia General de la Republica statement, 2026; resignations reported 1-2 May 2026

cases.n: The Culiacan municipal and police officials
cases.rank: mayor, police commanders and a senator
cases.d: Nine officials charged alongside the governor cover almost every layer of a single state: the mayor of the capital, a sitting senator, the state deputy attorney general, a former public security secretary and several police commanders. One is additionally charged over the kidnapping of a DEA source and a relative, both of whom died. The indictment describes a complete political and police protection network rather than individual corruption.
cases.cite: US v. Rocha Moya et al., S.D.N.Y., indictment unsealed 29 April 2026

cases.n: Rubilio Orlando Palacios — anti-drug police official
cases.d: The third official arrested with Guatemala's anti-drug chief and his deputy when all three travelled to the United States in 2005, charged in a three-count Washington indictment after a four-month DEA and Guatemalan investigation. The DEA administrator described them as Trojan horses for the addiction they were entrusted to prevent.
cases.cite: US District Court for the District of Columbia, indictment November 2005; pleas 2006

cases.n: The Fourth Criminal Court — Assad and the Fourth Division
cases.rank: head of state, division commander and security chiefs
cases.d: On 11 August 2026 the Fourth Criminal Court in Damascus sentenced the deposed president to death in absentia for premeditated murder, torture and crimes against humanity, and his brother, who commanded the Fourth Armoured Division, to death in absentia; six other officials received the same sentence in absentia. Only one defendant was present, a cousin who ran political security in Deraa and had been sanctioned by the US Treasury in 2011; he stood in a cage in prison uniform to hear it and has the right to appeal. Both brothers are in Russia with political asylum and Moscow has refused extradition. Opposition activists accuse the Fourth Division of killings, torture, extortion and drug trafficking, and Western and regional governments treat it as the backbone of state captagon manufacture — but the convictions are for war crimes, not the trade. Human Rights Watch opposed the sentences and questioned whether a fair trial was guaranteed.
cases.cite: Fourth Criminal Court, Damascus, judgment 11 August 2026, reported by SANA and international agencies; US Treasury designation of the Deraa political security head, April 2011; Human Rights Watch statement, August 2026

cases.n: Nouh Zeaiter — the four-month sentence
cases.rank: trafficker sanctioned by the US and EU
cases.d: Sanctioned by the United States and the United Kingdom in 2023 over captagon manufacture and smuggling alongside relatives and associates of the Assad family, and already convicted in absentia by a Lebanese military court in 2021, which gave him life with hard labour, and sentenced to death in absentia in March 2024 for shooting at soldiers, one of whom was killed. The army took him in an ambush near Baalbek in November 2025 and called him one of the most dangerous wanted men in the country. In February 2026 the military court sentenced him to four months, finding him guilty in four minor matters — arms trafficking, shootings, unlicensed weapons and wearing military clothing — with weapons and radios confiscated. He denied trafficking and said he grew cannabis only between 2005 and 2008. The same court that had already sentenced him twice in absentia reached four months once he was in front of it.
cases.cite: US and UK sanctions designations, 2023; Lebanese military court convictions in absentia, 2021 and March 2024; Lebanese Armed Forces arrest, 20 November 2025; military court sentence, February 2026

cases.n: Louay al-Yasiri — a governor's son, pardoned
cases.rank: son of a former governor, intelligence service employee
cases.d: Sentenced to life in 2018 for drug offences, the son of a former provincial governor and himself an employee of the intelligence service. He was later pardoned and released. It is the clearest documented instance of a trafficker with direct government connections reaching an Iraqi court, and the sentence did not hold. Against it stands the volume the same judiciary produces: over 14,000 arrests in 2024, 144 death sentences for international traffickers and 434 life sentences for local offenders, and 973 convictions in the first quarter of 2025 alone.
cases.cite: Iraqi court sentence, 2018, and subsequent pardon; Supreme Judicial Council and Ministry of Interior figures for 2024 and Q1 2025; UNODC seizure data

cases.n: Revolutionary Court judges in the drug docket
cases.d: Defence lawyers describe the courts that try drug cases as security-dominated and fast-tracking low-level defendants while leaving trafficking networks and higher-level operators untouched. One attorney who handled more than seventy drug cases documented the conduct of two named Tehran revolutionary court judges, one of whom he alleges was involved in financial corruption, and submitted a report with case files; lawyers who pursue such cases report being turned on themselves. With no independent forum, the allegation cannot be tested. Iran scores 9.50 on state-embedded actors, the joint highest on this map, and hangs hundreds of people a year for drug offences.
cases.cite: Center for Human Rights in Iran, testimony of a defence attorney and analysis of drug sentencing, April 2025; Iranian judiciary announcements via Mizan Online

cases.n: The tramadol trial — ten sentenced including security and intelligence officials
cases.d: A court in N'Djamena sentenced ten people on 24 July 2020 over a transnational tramadol network, among them high-ranking security and intelligence officials. Analysts reading the court documents described a network with strong Chadian connections and large sums circulating among its members, some of it used in attempts to corrupt the judiciary and the security services. The conviction is real and the assessment that followed it is the point: with senior army and intelligence figures involved, enforcement runs into the institutions expected to carry it out.
cases.cite: Court judgment, N'Djamena, 24 July 2020; Institute for Security Studies and ENACT analysis of the court documents, 2020; UNODC Sahel tramadol reporting, 2017

cases.n: A mayor and 200 kilograms in his vehicle
cases.d: A local mayor was arrested with more than 200 kilograms of cocaine in his vehicle, an incident cited in investigative-journalism guidance for Africa as the model case of why a seizure is only the start: the work is unravelling the network behind the office rather than recording the arrest. No outcome is documented here. Niger sits on the Sahel corridor UNODC describes as a natural stopover between South America and Europe, and reporting on it carries physical risk to journalists.
cases.cite: Global Investigative Journalism Network, Guide to Investigating Organized Crime in Africa, chapter on drug trafficking; UNODC Sahel trafficking assessments

cases.n: Tramadol supplied to the presidential guard
cases.rank: presidential guard and senior security officials
cases.d: Reporting from Bangui, drawing on researchers, dealers and a former employee of the group, describes remnants of the Wagner organisation supplying tramadol to members of the presidential guard and to a youth militia. Senior security officials are alleged to control the market, in which a consignment worth about $7,000 locally fetches up to $21,000 in Cameroon after roughly $4,000 is paid to Wagner and allied armed groups en route. A US-sponsored research centre assesses that the old Wagner has in effect taken over the state. Nothing has been charged. The country reports no update on an earlier case against a customs agent.
cases.cite: Wall Street Journal reporting from Bangui, 12 July 2026; GI-TOC Central Africa Observatory report, June 2026; Africa Center for Strategic Studies assessment; US State Department Trafficking in Persons Report, 2025

cases.n: Nicolas Maduro — head of state
cases.d: Charged in the Southern District of New York in March 2020 with narco-terrorism conspiracy, cocaine importation and weapons counts, alongside a group of serving and former officials. The State Department reward for information leading to his arrest was raised twice, reaching $50 million in 2025. No trial has taken place and none of the evidence has been tested in court; the indictment is an accusation, and this map does not treat it as more than that.
cases.cite: US v. Maduro Moros et al., S.D.N.Y., indictment March 2020; US Department of State Narcotics Rewards Program notices

cases.n: Diosdado Cabello — legislature president, later Interior Minister
cases.d: Designated by OFAC under the Kingpin Act in May 2018 and named in the 2020 SDNY indictment as a leader of the same structure. He has held the National Assembly presidency, the vice-presidency of the ruling party and, from 2024, the interior ministry. Both actions are executive and prosecutorial rather than judicial findings.
cases.cite: US Treasury OFAC Kingpin Act designation, May 2018; US v. Maduro Moros et al., S.D.N.Y., 2020

cases.n: Maher al-Assad — commander, Fourth Armoured Division
cases.d: The former president's brother, sanctioned by the United States, United Kingdom and European Union in 2023 over captagon production and export run through the division he commanded. The designations rest on intelligence findings and open-source investigation rather than a trial. After the government's collapse in December 2024 the production sites were opened to journalists and investigators, which corroborated the scale but not the individual attributions.
cases.cite: US Treasury OFAC and UK Foreign Office designations, March 2023; EU Council Implementing Regulation 2023/720; Centre for Operational Analysis and Research captagon reporting

cases.n: Porfirio Lobo Sosa — President 2010-2014
cases.d: Named by US prosecutors as a recipient of trafficking proceeds during the cases against his son and successor, and placed on the State Department's Engel list of corrupt actors in 2021. He has never been charged. The allegations come from cooperating witnesses in other people's trials, which is the weakest category of evidence on this map and is marked as such.
cases.cite: US Department of State section 353 corrupt and undemocratic actors list, July 2021; trial testimony in US v. Fabio Lobo and US v. Hernandez, S.D.N.Y.

cases.n: Testimony naming a sitting president
cases.d: Cooperating witnesses in the Guzman and Garcia Luna trials testified to bribes paid to a serving Mexican president. No charge has ever been brought, the testimony was not corroborated by documents, and the witnesses were negotiating their own sentences. It is recorded here because the claim was made under oath in a US federal court and because omitting it would misrepresent the trial record — not because it is established.
cases.cite: Trial testimony, US v. Guzman Loera, E.D.N.Y., 2019, and US v. Garcia Luna, E.D.N.Y., 2023

cases.n: President Joao Bernardo Vieira and the 2009 killings
cases.rank: head of state and armed forces chief
cases.d: The president and the army chief of staff were killed within hours of each other in March 2009, during the period when UNODC described the country as at risk of becoming Africa's first narco-state. No prosecution followed either killing. The link to the cocaine trade is the assessment of UNODC and of the UN Peacebuilding Support Office, not a court finding.
cases.cite: UNODC Transnational Organized Crime in West Africa; UN Security Council reporting on Guinea-Bissau, 2009-2012

cases.n: Nestor Reverol — head of the national anti-drug office, later Interior Minister
cases.d: Indicted in the Eastern District of New York in 2015 for allegedly warning traffickers of raids and obstructing seizures while running the national anti-drug office. He was promoted to Interior Minister the following year and later to the electricity ministry. The indictment remains unexecuted.
cases.cite: US v. Reverol Torres and Ordonez, E.D.N.Y., indictment 2015, unsealed August 2016

cases.n: Abdelghani Hamel — Director-General of National Security
cases.d: Removed after a 701-kilogram cocaine seizure at the port of Oran in May 2018 exposed the network behind it, and later convicted by a military court and by civilian courts on corruption and illicit enrichment counts.
