Several generals were convicted alongside him. The convictions are for corruption rather than narcotics, which is the record that exists; Algeria published little about the trafficking case itself.
cases.cite: Algerian Blida military tribunal and Tipaza court judgments, 2019-2020; Algerian Ministry of Justice statements

cases.n: Rana Sanaullah — provincial law minister
cases.d: Arrested by the Anti-Narcotics Force in July 2019 on a charge of transporting fifteen kilograms of heroin. The case collapsed and he was acquitted in 2022; the ANF officer who filed it later disowned the recovery. The episode is on this map as a documented instance of narcotics charges being deployed against a political opponent, which is a distinct failure mode from capture and belongs in the same record.
cases.cite: Pakistan Anti-Narcotics Force case records; Lahore Special Court acquittal, 2022; Islamabad High Court proceedings

cases.n: Abd al-Rahman Milad ('Bija') — coast guard commander
cases.d: A serving coast guard unit commander at Zawiya, sanctioned by the UN Security Council in June 2018 over fuel smuggling, migrant trafficking and violence at sea. He was detained in Libya in 2020 and released without conviction in 2021. The same coastal networks move hashish and pharmaceuticals; the UN designation covers the smuggling economy rather than narcotics specifically.
cases.cite: UN Security Council Committee on Libya sanctions listing, June 2018; UN Panel of Experts on Libya reports

cases.n: Army and border officers in the captagon cases
cases.d: Jordan's State Security Court has convicted serving and former soldiers of moving captagon and weapons across the Syrian border, in cases running from 2022 onward. The army also conducted airstrikes inside Syria against production and storage sites. The convictions are the clearest evidence on this corridor that the protection extends into the interdicting force itself.
cases.cite: Jordanian State Security Court judgments, 2022-2024; Jordanian Armed Forces statements

cases.n: The 2017 official 'drug barons' list
cases.d: The president read out a list of alleged drug traffickers in public in 2017 and ordered arrests; a regional commissioner and several public figures were named. Few prosecutions were completed and most of those detained were released. The episode is recorded as an assertion by a head of state, not as a set of findings.
cases.cite: Tanzanian government statements, February 2017; Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime East Africa reporting

cases.n: Officials named in the compound designations
cases.d: US and UK designations of Cambodian tycoons and companies over forced-labour fraud compounds have repeatedly described political protection as the reason the compounds operate openly. One designated figure was a serving senator. The designations are executive findings; Cambodian courts have prosecuted none of them.
cases.cite: US Treasury OFAC designations, December 2019, September 2024 and October 2025; UK sanctions designations

cases.n: Customs and border officials in the 2021 designations
cases.d: The largest single Magnitsky action ever taken against one country named Bulgarian officials and business figures, several of them in customs and border roles, over networks that included smuggling protection. Bulgarian prosecutions largely did not follow. The customs chokepoints on the Balkan route sit inside the same institutions.
cases.cite: US Treasury OFAC Global Magnitsky designations, June 2021; European Commission Rule of Law reports on Bulgaria

cases.n: State security links in the Belivuk prosecution
cases.d: The prosecution of the Belivuk-Miljkovic group produced evidence that its members held state security identification and had access to protected facilities, and a former head of the security service was later charged in connection with them. The case is running rather than concluded and the specific attributions remain contested in Serbian politics.
cases.cite: Serbian Special Prosecutor's Office for Organised Crime indictments, 2021-2024; Belgrade Higher Court proceedings

cases.n: Rinascita-Scott — the 'Ndrangheta maxi-trial
cases.d: Italy's largest organised crime trial since the Palermo maxi-trial: over 300 defendants, 207 convictions at first instance in November 2023. Those convicted included a former senator and lawyer who had acted for 'Ndrangheta figures, alongside police officers, officials and a former regional politician. Appeals are running.
cases.cite: Tribunale di Vibo Valentia, Rinascita-Scott judgment, November 2023; Italian Direzione Nazionale Antimafia reporting

cases.n: The judicial vetting
cases.d: An EU-monitored vetting of every judge and prosecutor in the country, running since 2017, has removed or forced out roughly half of those assessed, mostly on unexplained-wealth grounds. It is the largest deliberate purge of a judiciary attempted in Europe and the clearest admission by a state that its own courts had been captured. Individual outcomes are administrative rather than criminal.
cases.cite: Albanian Independent Qualification Commission and Special Appeal Chamber decisions; European Commission Albania progress reports

cases.n: A Ultranza Py — prosecutors and judges
cases.d: The 2022 investigation into a cocaine network moving product through the Hidrovia charged a serving prosecutor, court officials and figures connected to the legislature alongside the traffickers. One of the case's own prosecutors was later removed. Several principals fled before arrest.
cases.cite: Paraguayan Ministerio Publico, Operacion A Ultranza Py case file, 2022-2024; Paraguayan Jurado de Enjuiciamiento de Magistrados

cases.n: The dismantling of the anti-impunity capacity
cases.d: The UN-backed anti-impunity commission that produced most of the country's trafficking-linked prosecutions was expelled in 2019, and by 2023 more than thirty judges and prosecutors who had worked those cases had left the country under threat of arrest. The cases they built, several of them on this map, no longer have a domestic forum. This is capture achieved by removing the prosecutor rather than buying the judge.
cases.cite: UN International Commission against Impunity in Guatemala (CICIG) closure reporting, 2019; Inter-American Commission on Human Rights precautionary measures; US Department of State section 353 listings

cases.n: Jose Luis Abarca — mayor of Iguala
cases.d: Convicted of organised crime and kidnapping over the September 2014 disappearance of forty-three students, taken by municipal police acting for Guerreros Unidos. The Interdisciplinary Group of Independent Experts documented federal and state forces monitoring the events in real time. It remains the best-evidenced case on this map of a municipality operating as an arm of a trafficking organisation.
cases.cite: Mexican federal court judgments, 2019 and 2022; GIEI Ayotzinapa reports; Mexican Comision para la Verdad y Acceso a la Justicia, 2022

cases.n: Operacion Necora — Galicia
cases.d: The operation that exposed the Galician rias as Europe's principal cocaine landing zone, run by tobacco-smuggling clans that had converted to cocaine for the Medellin and Cali organisations. Convictions followed for several clan leaders; a substantial number of defendants were acquitted, and the political and municipal protection alleged at the time was never proven in court. The landing infrastructure it described is still in use.
cases.cite: Audiencia Nacional judgment, Operacion Necora, 1994; Spanish Fiscalia Antidroga historical reporting

cases.n: The Punjab synthetic drug racket
cases.rank: former deputy superintendent of police and political associates
cases.d: A former deputy superintendent of police was convicted over a synthetic drug network valued by Indian investigators in the hundreds of crores, in a case that reached into Punjab's political class through an associate of a serving minister. The wider political allegations were never proven; the police conviction was.
cases.cite: India Enforcement Directorate and Punjab Police case records; Special CBI Court, Mohali judgment

cases.n: Charges brought against a critic of the drug war
cases.d: A senator who had opened hearings into the killings was charged with drug offences in 2017 on the testimony of prison inmates and detained for almost seven years. Every charge was dismissed or ended in acquittal by 2023-2024 after witnesses recanted. This is the inverse of the pattern the rest of this layer records: not a state captured by the trade, but drug law used as an instrument against political opposition. Both are failures of the same institutions.
cases.cite: Philippine Regional Trial Court, Muntinlupa, dismissals and acquittals, 2021-2024; UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention Opinion 2018

cases.n: Militia and elected office in Rio de Janeiro
cases.d: The 2024 arrests over the 2018 killing of a Rio city councillor reached a serving federal deputy, his brother a former state accounts councillor, and a former head of the civil police's intelligence bureau. Rio's militias began as off-duty police protection rackets and now hold territory alongside the drug commands, taxing the same residents. The case is at indictment stage.
cases.cite: Brazilian Policia Federal and Procuradoria-Geral da Republica filings, March 2024; Supremo Tribunal Federal proceedings

cases.n: Allegations against a former interior minister
cases.d: A convicted organised crime figure published a long series of video statements from abroad in 2021 alleging that a former interior minister had protected trafficking networks, including a claim about a specific cocaine shipment. No charge followed in Turkiye and the allegations have never been tested. They are recorded because they were made publicly and in detail, and because the Susurluk file already on this map established the pattern they describe.
cases.cite: Public statements by Sedat Peker, 2021; Turkish parliamentary opposition motions; no prosecution filed

cases.n: A legislator arrested in a narcotics operation
cases.d: A sitting deputy of the governing coalition was arrested in a police operation involving a cocaine sample, then released; parliamentary immunity was lifted and the case did not proceed to a verdict. Senegal's ports and airport sit on the West African route and the case is the only one to have reached the legislature.
cases.cite: Senegalese Division des Investigations Criminelles case records, 2019; Senegalese National Assembly immunity proceedings

cases.n: The 30th Precinct — New York
cases.d: Thirty-three officers of one Harlem precinct were arrested for robbing dealers, reselling seized cocaine and perjury. Around 125 convictions were vacated. The Mollen Commission, reporting the same year, found that the department's internal affairs function had been structured to avoid finding what it eventually found.
cases.cite: Mollen Commission Report on Police Corruption, City of New York, July 1994; S.D.N.Y. prosecutions, 1994-1996

cases.n: Rampart CRASH — Los Angeles
cases.d: An anti-gang unit that planted evidence, shot unarmed people and dealt in seized narcotics. More than 100 convictions were overturned and the city entered a federal consent decree that ran for twelve years. Several officers were convicted; several convictions were later reversed on appeal, which is part of the record.
cases.cite: Los Angeles Board of Inquiry into the Rampart Area Corruption Incident, 2000; US v. City of Los Angeles consent decree, 2001

cases.n: The Miami River Cops
cases.d: Officers of the Miami Police Department robbed cocaine loads from the river and resold them; three men drowned fleeing one raid. Nineteen officers were convicted after three federal trials. The department had expanded rapidly in the preceding years with reduced screening, which the subsequent review identified as the enabling condition.
cases.cite: US v. Garcia et al., S.D. Fla., 1986-1988; City of Miami internal review, 1988

cases.n: Customs and Border Protection corruption
cases.d: The largest federal law enforcement agency in the country records a continuous stream of officer prosecutions for waving loads through ports of entry, running to more than 200 corruption convictions across a decade. The agency's own integrity advisory panel found the internal affairs staffing inadequate to the caseload and said so in public.
cases.cite: CBP Integrity Advisory Panel final report, 2016; CBP Office of Professional Responsibility annual statistics; DOJ prosecution records

cases.n: The Philadelphia narcotics field unit
cases.d: Six officers were tried federally for robbing dealers and falsifying reports and were acquitted in 2015. The city nonetheless vacated around 1,000 convictions the unit had produced and paid several million dollars in civil settlements. An acquittal and a mass vacatur in the same case is the clearest illustration on this map of how differently the criminal and civil standards resolve.
cases.cite: US v. Liciardello et al., E.D. Pa., verdict May 2015; Philadelphia District Attorney's Office conviction review; city civil settlements

cases.n: The Camden narcotics squad
cases.d: Officers planted drugs and fabricated reports; around 200 cases were dismissed and the city later dissolved its police department entirely and rebuilt it under county control. It is one of very few instances anywhere on this map of an institution being abolished rather than reformed.
cases.cite: US v. Bayard et al., D.N.J., 2010; New Jersey Attorney General review; City of Camden police dissolution, 2013

cases.n: Operation Tiberius — the Metropolitan Police
cases.d: An internal Metropolitan Police report, written in 2002 and leaked in 2014, concluded that organised crime networks had been able to infiltrate the force at will, naming officers connected to specific families. It was never published, no prosecutions followed from it, and its findings have not been tested in any forum. It is the most senior internal assessment of its kind in a Western police service.
cases.cite: Metropolitan Police Operation Tiberius report, 2002 (leaked 2014); UK Home Affairs Select Committee questioning, 2014

cases.n: Eirik Jensen — head of the Oslo police narcotics unit
cases.d: The officer who ran Oslo's narcotics section for years was convicted of aggravated corruption and of complicity in importing around fourteen tonnes of hashish with an informant he had run, and sentenced to twenty-one years. The Supreme Court refused his appeal in 2021. It is the most senior police conviction of its kind in Scandinavia.
cases.cite: Oslo District Court 2017 and Borgarting Court of Appeal 2020 judgments; Norwegian Supreme Court refusal, 2021

cases.n: Police and security service leaks to the networks
cases.rank: police employees and a security service officer
cases.d: Swedish courts have convicted police employees of passing information from law enforcement registers to criminal networks, and separately convicted a Security Service officer of unauthorised disclosure. Police reporting names insider access to registers as a systematic vulnerability rather than an isolated failure.
cases.cite: Swedish district court judgments, 2021-2024; Polismyndigheten and Sakerhetspolisen public reporting

cases.n: Customs and port officers at the northern terminals
cases.d: Prosecutions at Hamburg and Bremerhaven have convicted customs officers and terminal employees of clearing containers and passing scanner information. German federal police assessments treat port-side insider access as the decisive vulnerability in the northern European cocaine flow, as Belgian and Dutch assessments do for Antwerp and Rotterdam.
cases.cite: Hamburg and Bremen Landgericht judgments, 2020-2024; Bundeskriminalamt Rauschgiftkriminalitat Bundeslagebild

cases.n: The BAC Nord case — Marseille
cases.d: Officers of the northern Marseille anti-crime brigade were charged with stealing seized cannabis, money and phones from the estates they policed. Convictions followed after a long procedural fight; several charges fell away. The estates in question are the same ones on this map's group layer.
cases.cite: Tribunal correctionnel de Marseille judgments, 2015-2021; Inspection generale de la police nationale reporting

cases.n: The Vught escape plot
cases.d: Prosecutors alleged a plan to free the principal defendant in the Marengo trial from the country's highest-security prison, involving contacts around the legal and custodial system. It followed the murders of the trial's crown witness's brother, his lawyer and a journalist. The Dutch state's response was to harden the prison regime, which is a measure of how far the threat was assessed to reach.
cases.cite: Dutch Openbaar Ministerie statements and Rechtbank Amsterdam proceedings, 2022-2024

cases.n: The Noor 1 case
cases.d: Two tonnes of heroin arrived at Piraeus aboard a tanker and part of the load disappeared before it was secured. Convictions followed for the vessel's operators and associates; the Greek parliament held hearings on how the load moved through the port. It remains the largest single seizure in Greek history and the case that established Piraeus as an entry point rather than a transit stop.
cases.cite: Greek Court of Appeal judgments, 2016-2019; Hellenic Parliament committee proceedings

cases.n: Police leaks to criminal organisations
cases.d: Israeli courts have convicted serving officers of passing investigative material to crime organisations, in cases brought by the justice ministry's police investigations department. The organisations receiving the material are the same families mapped in the group layer.
cases.cite: Israeli Department for Investigation of Police Officers (Mahash) case records; district court judgments, 2019-2024

cases.n: Carabineros narcotics units
cases.d: Chilean prosecutors have charged officers of the Carabineros with reselling seized narcotics and protecting distribution in Santiago and the northern border region, in a series of cases running alongside the institution's wider post-2019 crisis. Chile's role shifted in this period from consumer market to transit route.
cases.cite: Chilean Fiscalia Nacional and Fiscalia de Alta Complejidad case records, 2020-2024

cases.n: Narcotics police and enforcement officers
cases.d: Malaysia's anti-corruption commission has prosecuted narcotics officers for releasing suspects and reselling seized product, in cases concentrated in Johor and the Klang valley. The country sits on the Golden Triangle export route and hosts the region's busiest transhipment port.
cases.cite: Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission prosecution records, 2018-2024; Malaysian sessions court judgments

cases.n: Police and political links in the Madush case
cases.d: The arrest in Dubai of a Sri Lankan trafficking figure produced photographs of him with police officers, entertainers and politicians at a party, triggering suspensions and an inquiry. He was killed in police custody in 2020 before any of it was tested. The inquiry did not conclude.
cases.cite: Sri Lanka Police Special Investigation Unit reporting, 2019-2020; Sri Lankan Human Rights Commission inquiry into the custodial death

cases.n: The Teknaf yaba campaign and its aftermath
cases.d: The anti-drug campaign on the Myanmar border produced hundreds of killings in police custody or 'crossfire'. A former officer-in-charge of the Teknaf station and several colleagues were sentenced to death in 2022 for the killing of a retired army major who had filmed them. The convictions are for murder; the drug economy the campaign targeted was not disrupted.
cases.cite: Cox's Bazar District and Sessions Judge Court verdict, January 2022; UN OHCHR statements on Bangladesh drug operations

cases.n: The drug war killings
cases.d: Between 6,000 and more than 30,000 people were killed in anti-drug operations from 2016, depending on whether the count is the government's or that of human rights monitors. The International Criminal Court authorised an investigation into them as crimes against humanity in 2021, and the former president was surrendered to the Court in 2025. The trade itself continued through the campaign.
cases.cite: ICC Pre-Trial Chamber authorisation, September 2021, and arrest warrant proceedings, 2025; UN OHCHR report on the Philippines, 2020

cases.n: Border and law enforcement officers
cases.d: Australian courts have convicted Border Force and state police officers of assisting importations through Sydney and Melbourne, in cases brought after the law enforcement integrity commission's referrals. Australia pays the highest wholesale prices of any market on this map, which is what the insider is being paid against.
cases.cite: Australian Commission for Law Enforcement Integrity annual reports and referrals; NSW and Victorian court judgments, 2016-2024

cases.n: Border services officers
cases.d: Canada Border Services Agency officers have been convicted of waving vehicles through at the Windsor-Detroit and Pacific Highway crossings. The agency had no independent civilian oversight body until legislation was brought forward in the 2020s, which is unusual among comparable agencies.
cases.cite: Ontario and British Columbia court judgments, 2014-2023; CBSA internal affairs reporting; Public Safety Canada oversight legislation

cases.n: Senior police and the protection economy
cases.d: The deputy national police chief was removed and investigated in 2023 over an alleged protection relationship with an online gambling network, in a case that split the police leadership publicly. The charges concern gambling proceeds rather than narcotics, but the protection mechanism and the laundering rails are the same ones the trade uses.
cases.cite: Royal Thai Police disciplinary proceedings and Thai Office of the Attorney-General filings, 2023-2024

cases.n: Officers at the western crossings
cases.d: Ukrainian anti-corruption bodies have charged customs and border service officers at the Zakarpattia crossings with running contraband channels into the European Union. The charges concern smuggling generally rather than narcotics specifically; the crossings are the same ones used by the eastern corridor on this map's route layer.
cases.cite: Ukrainian National Anti-Corruption Bureau and State Bureau of Investigation case records, 2022-2024

cases.n: Jimmy Cherizier — former police officer, sanctioned gang leader
cases.d: A serving officer of the Haitian National Police until 2018, subsequently the leader of the largest federation of armed groups in Port-au-Prince and the first individual designated under the UN's Haiti sanctions regime in 2022. The trajectory from the force to the federation, rather than any single act, is what this entry records.
cases.cite: UN Security Council Resolution 2653 designation, October 2022; US and Canadian sanctions designations; UN Panel of Experts on Haiti reports

entities.role: Retail bank — branch staff and compliance
entities.d: The first bank in US history to plead guilty to conspiracy to commit money laundering. It admitted three networks moved more than $670 million through its accounts over six years against $18.3 trillion in unmonitored activity. Employees including a store manager were bribed; one took $11,000 in retail gift cards. Penalties totalled about $3.09 billion, with an asset cap on its US units.
entities.cite: US v. TD Bank NA, D.N.J., guilty plea October 2024

entities.d: Convicted by the Swiss Federal Criminal Court of failing to prevent money laundering by a Bulgarian cocaine-trafficking organisation, alongside a former relationship manager. The first criminal conviction of a major Swiss bank in the country's history.
entities.cite: Bundesstrafgericht / Tribunal pénal fédéral, Bellinzona, June 2022

entities.d: Deferred prosecution and $1.9 billion after US authorities found its Mexican affiliate had moved Sinaloa and Norte del Valle proceeds through bulk cash deposits its monitoring did not catch. No individual executive was prosecuted; the DPA expired without charges.
entities.cite: US v. HSBC Bank USA NA, E.D.N.Y., DPA December 2012

entities.d: Between 2004 and 2007 the bank took some $378 billion from thirteen Mexican currency exchange houses through correspondent accounts, money used among other things to buy aircraft for trafficking. In March 2010 it entered a deferred prosecution agreement in the Southern District of Florida: $110 million forfeited and a $50 million fine, at the time the largest penalty ever imposed for a Bank Secrecy Act violation. Charges were dismissed a year later on compliance with the agreement. No executive was prosecuted, and the sum is a fraction of one year's profit at the bank.
entities.cite: US v. Wachovia Bank N.A., S.D. Fla., deferred prosecution agreement approved 17 March 2010, Case No. 10-20165-CR-LENARD; consent agreements with the OCC and FinCEN; Wells Fargo Form 8-K, 17 March 2010

entities.d: The California subsidiary of the Dutch bank pleaded guilty in February 2018 to a felony conspiracy charge and paid $368.7 million, the largest financial penalty in the Southern District of California. The offence is not the laundering itself: the bank admitted conspiring with former executives to obstruct an examination by its regulator, concealing the deficiencies in its anti-money-laundering programme after learning that large numbers of customer transactions indicated trafficking and organised crime. A former vice-president had taken a deferred prosecution agreement two months earlier and was cooperating.
entities.cite: US v. Rabobank National Association, S.D. Cal., guilty plea 7 February 2018 before Magistrate Judge Jill Burkhardt; Department of Justice statement; deferred prosecution agreement with a former vice-president, 14 December 2017

entities.d: Forfeited $97 million under a non-prosecution agreement over failures in monitoring remittances to Mexico, where a small compliance staff generated fewer than ten suspicious activity reports against millions of transactions flagged by its own systems.
entities.cite: US DOJ non-prosecution agreement, May 2017

entities.d: Pleaded guilty to bank fraud conspiracy and forfeited $2 billion over roughly €200 billion in non-resident flows through a single branch. Laundering infrastructure rather than drug-specific: the same channel serves any proceeds needing distance from their origin.
entities.cite: US v. Danske Bank A/S, S.D.N.Y., plea December 2022

entities.d: The company entered a deferred prosecution agreement on 19 January 2017 admitting willful failure to maintain an effective anti-money-laundering programme and aiding and abetting wire fraud between 2004 and 2012, and forfeited $586 million — the largest forfeiture ever imposed on a money services business — to be used to reimburse defrauded consumers. The specific failure is the one worth recording: it filed suspicious activity reports about its customers but not about its own agents, whom it knew were complicit. Prosecutors said employees fought to keep high-volume agents because of their turnover. Twenty-six agents in the United States and Canada had already been convicted since 2001. New York fined the company a further $60 million in 2018 and France penalised it in 2019.
entities.cite: US Department of Justice and Federal Trade Commission deferred prosecution agreement and consent order, 19 January 2017, with the US Attorneys for the Middle and Eastern Districts of Pennsylvania, the Central District of California and the Southern District of Florida; FinCEN civil money penalty; New York Department of Financial Services penalty, 2018

entities.d: Paid an A$1.3 billion civil penalty, the largest in Australian history, over roughly 23 million reporting breaches. Cited here as scale evidence on monitoring failure rather than as a drug case.
entities.cite: AUSTRAC v. Westpac Banking Corporation, Federal Court of Australia, 2020

entities.d: Settled with Dutch prosecutors for €775 million after clients used its accounts for laundering over years while customer due diligence was under-resourced. No individuals were charged, a decision later challenged in the Dutch courts.
entities.cite: Openbaar Ministerie settlement, September 2018

entities.d: Named by FinCEN as a primary money-laundering concern; the designation triggered a deposit run and the bank's self-liquidation within weeks. A demonstration that designation can end an institution without a trial.
entities.cite: FinCEN Section 311 notice of proposed rulemaking, February 2018

entities.d: FinCEN found in March 2015 that high-level managers had knowingly processed transactions for third-party launderers acting for transnational criminal organisations, moving hundreds of millions through four US correspondent banks. Andorra took over the bank the next day and wound it up within the week, splitting it into a continuing bank and a bad bank; clients had to prove their own funds legitimate to recover them. In July 2025 a court sentenced eighteen executives, the former chief executive to seven years and a 30 million euro fine. The defendants are appealing, and shareholders argue the bank was closed on an administrative finding without evidence tested in court. Some clients named in the case have never been convicted.
entities.cite: FinCEN Section 311 notice of finding, 10 March 2015; Andorran intervention and liquidation, March 2015; Andorran court sentences, July 2025

entities.d: Pleaded guilty to Bank Secrecy Act and sanctions violations and agreed to $4.3 billion in penalties; its founder pleaded guilty personally. Filings describe transactions with darknet markets and ransomware actors passing through with no effective monitoring.
entities.cite: US v. Binance Holdings Ltd, W.D. Wash., plea November 2023

entities.d: An exchange indicted as a laundering vehicle for roughly $4 billion, including narcotics proceeds; its operator was arrested in Greece, convicted in France, and later pleaded guilty in the United States.
entities.cite: US v. BTC-e and Vinnik, N.D. Cal., indictment 2017; US plea 2024

entities.d: Seized by German police with its servers and about €23 million in bitcoin, and sanctioned by the US Treasury the same day. It was the largest darknet drug marketplace, with laundering services sold alongside the product.
entities.cite: BKA seizure and OFAC designation, April 2022

entities.d: Sanctioned by OFAC as a laundering tool; a developer was convicted in the Netherlands in 2024. The US designation was later vacated in part on appeal, leaving the question of whether software can be sanctioned unresolved.
entities.cite: OFAC designation August 2022; Van der Linde ruling, Rechtbank Oost-Brabant, 2024; Van Loon v. Treasury, 5th Cir., 2024

entities.n: MSC Gayane — 20 tonnes and the crew list
entities.role: Container vessel — chief mate, second mate and crew
entities.d: Roughly 20 tonnes of cocaine were seized from a Mediterranean Shipping Company vessel in Philadelphia in 2019, the largest such seizure in US history at the time. Eight seafarers pleaded guilty, among them the chief mate and second mate, drawing about 50 years between them; the ship was released after the operator posted security. The cargo was not loaded at an export terminal but taken aboard at night at sea, which puts the vulnerability in the crew list rather than the container manifest. The operator called itself a victim and said it was spending over 00 million on security in response.
entities.cite: US v. Vasquez Reyes, Penda, Ilic, Kavaja and others, E.D. Pa., pleas and sentences 2019-2022

entities.n: Port of Antwerp — terminal access and scanning data
entities.role: Container terminals — hiring, gate systems and scan records
entities.d: Antwerp handles the largest cocaine volumes in Europe, and the terminal operators sit at the point of attack: container reference codes, gate access and scanning records are commercial systems, and the people with them are recruited rather than the cargo intercepted. Seizures reached 116 tonnes in 2023 alone. The port authority and operators have since restricted access and rotated codes; the EU review of port corruption found the vulnerability is staff access rather than screening technology.
entities.cite: Antwerp port authority and terminal operator measures, 2022-2024; EUDA and World Customs Organization joint report, 2025

entities.d: Prosecutions of container extraction crews, including cases where terminal employees supplied PIN codes from the port's own release system. The vulnerability is administrative access rather than physical security.
entities.cite: Rotterdam District Court proceedings, multiple, 2019–2024

entities.d: Ecuador's cocaine exports move inside legitimate fruit shipments; national seizure volumes rose alongside export growth, and prosecutions have reached exporters, port staff and customs officials. Ecuador's criminality score rose to 7.48 in the 2025 Index.
entities.cite: Fiscalia General del Estado prosecutions; UNODC seizure reporting

entities.n: Amarvel Biotech and other PRC precursor suppliers
entities.d: US indictments charged China-based chemical companies and their executives with trafficking fentanyl precursors, alleging they marketed the chemicals to Mexican buyers and advised on concealing shipments. The companies are outside US jurisdiction in practice.
entities.cite: US v. Amarvel Biotech et al., S.D.N.Y., indictments June 2023

entities.d: The reagent required to convert morphine into heroin is a mainstream industrial chemical. The INCB tracks legitimate trade and repeatedly reports diversion at the distribution layer rather than at manufacture, which is where controls are weakest.
entities.cite: INCB Precursors Report, annual

entities.d: The three largest US drug distributors agreed to pay about $21 billion over 18 years to settle claims that they shipped opioid volumes their own monitoring systems flagged. Diversion out of a licensed supply chain, not capture by an outside group.
entities.cite: National Prescription Opiate Litigation, N.D. Ohio, settlement July 2021

entities.d: Pleaded guilty to three felonies including conspiracy to defraud the United States and violating the anti-kickback statute, with $8.3 billion in penalties. The Sackler settlement structure was rejected by the Supreme Court in 2024 and renegotiated.
entities.cite: US v. Purdue Pharma LP, D.N.J., plea November 2020; Harrington v. Purdue Pharma, 2024

entities.d: The first US distributor charged criminally over opioid diversion; its former chief executive was later convicted. Establishing personal criminal liability at this layer took two decades of the epidemic.
entities.cite: US v. Rochester Drug Co-Operative, S.D.N.Y., deferred prosecution 2019; US v. Doud, conviction 2022

entities.d: Its chairman was convicted in Macau of running a criminal syndicate and illegal gambling and sentenced to 18 years. Junket credit systems moved value across borders in a form that generated no bank record.
entities.cite: Court of First Instance, Macau SAR, January 2023

entities.d: A NSW commission found the company unsuitable to hold a licence after evidence that junket partners with organised-crime links used its accounts to move funds; AUSTRAC later obtained a A$450 million penalty.
entities.cite: Bergin Inquiry report, February 2021; AUSTRAC v. Crown, Federal Court, 2023

entities.d: Forfeited $130 million to resolve allegations it let unlicensed money transmitting move funds for foreign patrons. The mechanism was informal value transfer routed around the banking system entirely.
entities.cite: US DOJ non-prosecution agreement, September 2024

entities.d: The firm at the centre of the Panama Papers; its founders and 26 others were acquitted of money laundering by a Panamanian court in 2024, the judge citing insufficient and improperly gathered evidence. The acquittal is the record and belongs on the map as much as a conviction would.
entities.cite: Duodécimo Juzgado Penal, Panama, verdict June 2024

entities.n: UK company formation — Scottish Limited Partnerships
entities.d: Structures registered in the UK for a few pounds, with no verified beneficial owner until recent reform, appeared repeatedly in laundering schemes traced by journalists and regulators. Not a firm but a jurisdictional product, and the reason gatekeeper prosecutions are so rare.
entities.cite: UK Government SLP consultation and reform; Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023

entities.d: Its chief executive pleaded guilty to running a criminal enterprise, the first US prosecution of a company for knowingly supplying encrypted devices to trafficking organisations. Devices were sold with the camera and microphone removed.
entities.cite: US v. Ramos, S.D. Cal., plea October 2018

entities.d: Its chief executive was indicted in the United States for racketeering; Belgian and Dutch police had already penetrated the network, producing about a billion messages that underpinned hundreds of European prosecutions. Five years on the charges remain untried: the company’s distributor spent four years in a French jail before release on bail in 2025 and awaits a trial listed for late 2026, and both men maintain their innocence. The evidence the takedown produced has convicted hundreds of others in the meantime.
entities.cite: US v. Eap, S.D. Cal., indictment March 2021; Belgian federal police operation, March 2021; French proceedings against the distributor, bail June 2025, trial listed late 2026

entities.d: French and Dutch authorities compromised the network's servers in 2020. The resulting material produced thousands of arrests across Europe and remains the single largest evidentiary source in modern European organised-crime prosecutions; its admissibility has been litigated in several countries.
entities.cite: Operation Emma/Lemont, Eurojust, 2020; national admissibility rulings 2021–2024

entities.d: Three traders were convicted or pleaded guilty over a scheme importing roughly $3.6 billion in illegally mined South American gold, laundering drug proceeds through metal purchases. Gold converts cash into an exportable commodity with a legitimate invoice.
entities.cite: US v. Barrage, Granda and Rodriguez, S.D. Fla., pleas 2017–2018

entities.d: Pleaded guilty in US federal court to making payments to the AUC, a designated terrorist organisation and one of Colombia's largest cocaine traffickers, and paid a $25 million fine. A Florida jury found the company liable in a civil case brought by victims' families in 2024.
entities.cite: US v. Chiquita Brands International, D.D.C., plea March 2007; civil verdict S.D. Fla., June 2024

entities.n: Dubai gold trade — Kaloti and the refining chain
entities.role: Gold refining and bullion trading — cash purchase
entities.d: A DEA-led task force spent three years assembling a case against one of the world’s largest gold traders and refiners, concluding it bought metal from sellers suspected of laundering for drug traffickers, often paying cash and wiring funds for suspect clients. Treasury abandoned the case. An auditor’s 2012 inspection had already found .2 billion in cash-for-gold deals, about 45 percent of the firm’s business that year, and 2.4 tonnes taken in more than a thousand transactions from customers who provided no paperwork; the partner who reported it was forced out and sued his firm. Dubai’s regulator removed the refinery from its approved list in 2015. The company denies the allegations and continues to trade.
entities.cite: Ernst & Young inspection report, 2012, and whistleblower disclosure, 2014; DMCC delisting, 2015; ICIJ FinCEN Files reporting on the abandoned Treasury case, 2020-2024

entities.role: Retail and correspondent bank — used-car trade finance
entities.d: Named by FinCEN as a primary money-laundering concern for moving proceeds of a cocaine network that shipped through West Africa and settled its accounts by buying used cars in the United States for resale in Africa. The bank's assets were sold and its successor forfeited $102 million; no banker was prosecuted.
entities.cite: FinCEN Section 311 finding, February 2011; US v. Lebanese Canadian Bank SAL, S.D.N.Y., settlement August 2013

entities.d: Designated by OFAC alongside its owners, a former vice-president's family, as a laundering vehicle for the Cachiros trafficking organisation. Honduran regulators put it into liquidation within days of the designation, and depositors were paid out over the following year.
entities.cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, October 2015; CNBS liquidation order, October 2015

entities.d: Designated by FinCEN over accounts held for North Korean entities, including proceeds described as coming from narcotics and counterfeit currency. The action froze roughly $25 million and cut the bank out of dollar clearing; it is the clearest demonstration that a designation reaches further than a prosecution.
entities.cite: FinCEN Section 311 finding, September 2005; final rule 2007

entities.d: Registered in Tanzania and operated from Cyprus, it was named by FinCEN as a primary money-laundering concern over accounts used by organised crime and sanctioned parties. Cyprus resolved the bank; the owners' arbitration against the designation ran for years afterwards.
entities.cite: FinCEN Section 311 notice, July 2014; final rule 2016

entities.d: Deferred prosecution and $613 million in penalties after admitting it capped the number of alerts its monitoring software could generate so that the workload matched the size of its compliance staff. The bank also failed to report a customer running an unlicensed payday lending business.
entities.cite: US v. U.S. Bank National Association, S.D.N.Y., DPA February 2018

entities.d: Fined $390 million by FinCEN over its Check Cashing Group unit, which processed roughly $16 billion for clients including businesses whose organised-crime associations the bank's own files had recorded. The relationships continued for years after the warnings.
entities.cite: FinCEN consent order, January 2021

entities.d: A 2012 deferred prosecution and $100 million forfeiture over agents processing fraud and structured transfers was followed in 2018 by a further $125 million when the company was found to have breached the agreement's terms. The agent model puts the compliance duty on thousands of small franchises and the penalty on the brand.
entities.cite: US v. MoneyGram International Inc., M.D. Pa., DPA November 2012; amended settlement November 2018

entities.d: Fined about $630 million by US and UK regulators over mirror trades that moved roughly $10 billion out of Russia through its Moscow, London and New York desks, and a further $150 million by New York in 2020 for onboarding failures. Laundering infrastructure rather than a drug case: the same channel carries any proceeds that need distance from their origin.
entities.cite: NYDFS and FCA consent orders, January 2017; NYDFS consent order, July 2020

entities.d: Fined 4 billion kronor by the Swedish regulator over high-risk non-resident flows through its Estonian, Latvian and Lithuanian branches and misleading disclosures about them. The Baltic corridor's laundering capacity outlived the Danske case by several years.
entities.cite: Finansinspektionen decision, March 2020

entities.d: Settled with Dutch prosecutors for €480 million after admitting years of failures in customer checks and reporting. Three former executives were separately named as suspects, which is rare: in most cases at this scale the institution pays and no individual is charged.
entities.cite: Openbaar Ministerie settlement, April 2021

entities.d: The first large anonymous drug marketplace, handling several hundred million dollars in sales before its seizure in 2013. Its operator was convicted on seven counts and sentenced to life without parole in 2015; he was pardoned in January 2025 and released.
entities.cite: US v. Ulbricht, S.D.N.Y., verdict February 2015, sentence May 2015; presidential pardon January 2025
entities.undone: Operator pardoned by the US president in January 2025 and released from a life sentence.

entities.d: Ten times the size of Silk Road at its peak and seized in a joint operation in July 2017. Its administrator was arrested in Bangkok and died in custody a week later, which ended the prosecution before any of the evidence was tested.
entities.cite: US Department of Justice and Europol operation, July 2017; S.D. Fla. indictment

entities.d: Dutch police took over the market's servers and ran it themselves for 27 days, collecting addresses and passwords from users fleeing the AlphaBay seizure. The tactic reversed the usual sequence: the takedown came after the surveillance rather than instead of it.
entities.cite: Dutch National Police and Europol, Operation Bayonet, July 2017

entities.d: Three German administrators were arrested in 2019 after attempting to abscond with roughly €11 million held in escrow. They were convicted in Germany; a US indictment named them and two prolific vendors.
entities.cite: Landgericht Kleve proceedings, verdicts 2021; C.D. Cal. indictment, May 2019

entities.d: A mixing service that laundered roughly 350,000 bitcoin, much of it from darknet drug markets it partnered with directly. Its operator pleaded guilty to a laundering conspiracy and was fined $60 million by FinCEN — the first such penalty against a mixer.
entities.cite: US v. Harmon, D.D.C., plea August 2021; FinCEN civil penalty, October 2020

entities.d: The longest-running mixing service, moving about 1.2 million bitcoin over a decade, a large share of it darknet drug proceeds. Its operator was convicted at trial in March 2024 on blockchain analysis that reached back to transactions made in 2011.
entities.cite: US v. Sterlingov, D.D.C., verdict March 2024, sentence November 2024

entities.d: Named by FinCEN as a primary money-laundering concern in the first use of a new sanctions authority. Officials described over $700 million in transfers with Hydra alone between 2018 and 2022, in both directions: buyers funded purchases from Bitzlato accounts and vendors sent the takings back to them.
entities.cite: FinCEN order under Section 9714(a), January 2023; US v. Legkodymov, E.D.N.Y.

entities.d: Sanctioned by OFAC in April 2022 for processing proceeds from Hydra and ransomware operators. Estonia had already withdrawn its licence; the exchange kept operating from Moscow, which is the practical limit of designating an entity inside a jurisdiction that will not act on it.
entities.cite: OFAC designation, April 2022; Estonian FIU licence revocation, February 2022

entities.d: German and US authorities seized the service's servers and about €44 million in bitcoin, citing roughly $700 million in laundered funds from darknet markets and ransomware. It broke deposits into uniform chips so that no output amount could be matched to an input.
entities.cite: BKA and US Department of Justice seizure, March 2023

entities.d: A market that sold prescription pills, many of them counterfeit and fentanyl-laced, and closed by extorting its own users with the threat of publishing their transaction records. Its operator was arrested at JFK in May 2024 and charged in Manhattan.
entities.cite: US v. Rui-Siang Lin, S.D.N.Y., complaint May 2024

entities.role: Container terminals — dock and clearance staff
entities.d: Sixteen tonnes of cocaine hidden in tins of putty were found in a single Hamburg container in February 2021, the largest seizure in Europe at the time. German prosecutions have reached dock workers and hauliers; volumes rose here as Antwerp and Rotterdam hardened, which is displacement rather than growth.
entities.cite: German customs (Zoll) seizure announcement, February 2021; Hamburg court proceedings

entities.d: Italy's largest transhipment port sits in the province the 'Ndrangheta holds most completely. Anti-mafia investigations have documented control over hiring and container handling; the seizure figures published each year are the visible fraction of what moves through it.
entities.cite: Direzione Investigativa Antimafia semi-annual reports; Reggio Calabria DDA proceedings

entities.d: A father and son were indicted in Ohio and designated by OFAC as a fentanyl trafficking organisation that manufactured analogues to order and shipped them by post to buyers in at least 25 countries. Both remain in China; the case established the pattern the later precursor indictments follow.
entities.cite: US v. Fujing Zheng and Guanghua Zheng, N.D. Ohio, indictment 2018; OFAC designation August 2019

entities.n: Indian opioid exports to West Africa
entities.d: An investigation traced tapentadol and carisoprodol combinations, unapproved for sale in either the exporting or the importing country, from Indian manufacturers to street markets in Ghana, Nigeria and Cote d'Ivoire. India's drug regulator suspended export permissions and inspected the plants named; the companies deny wrongdoing.
entities.cite: BBC Eye investigation, February 2025; CDSCO enforcement action, 2025

entities.role: Manufacturer — sales force and prior authorisation
entities.d: The founder and four executives were convicted of racketeering for bribing prescribers to write a fentanyl spray licensed only for cancer breakthrough pain, and running a unit that lied to insurers to get the prescriptions covered. The founder was sentenced to 66 months; the company filed for bankruptcy days after pleading guilty.
entities.cite: US v. Kapoor et al., D. Mass., verdict May 2019, sentence January 2020

entities.d: The three chains agreed to pay about $13.8 billion over 15 years to settle claims that their pharmacies filled opioid prescriptions their own systems had flagged. A federal jury had already found the three liable for creating a public nuisance in two Ohio counties.
entities.cite: National Prescription Opiate Litigation, N.D. Ohio, settlements November 2022; Lake and Trumbull County verdict, November 2021

entities.d: The largest US manufacturer of generic oxycodone agreed to $1.7 billion in opioid settlement payments through its bankruptcy, having earlier paid $35 million to resolve DEA findings that it failed to report suspicious orders. Its output at one point exceeded the rest of the generic market combined.
entities.cite: In re Mallinckrodt plc, D. Del., plan confirmed 2022; DEA administrative settlement 2017

entities.d: Teva agreed to about $4.25 billion in cash and generic naloxone supply to settle US opioid claims, and Allergan to $2.37 billion. Neither admitted wrongdoing, and the naloxone component means part of the settlement is paid in the antidote to the product.
entities.cite: National opioid settlements announced November and July 2022

entities.d: Resolved US charges for $600 million after a subsidiary pleaded guilty to a felony over marketing an opioid dependence film as safer around children than it had evidence to claim. Its former parent paid $1.4 billion separately, and its former chief executive pleaded guilty to a misdemeanour.
entities.cite: US v. Indivior Solutions, W.D. Va., plea July 2020; Reckitt Benckiser resolution 2019

entities.d: A NSW inquiry found the company unsuitable to hold its Sydney licence after evidence it disguised gambling spend as hotel expenses on China UnionPay cards and extended large credit lines to patrons whose organised-crime links had been reported internally. AUSTRAC took it to the Federal Court over 117 high-risk patrons and its dealings with the Suncity junket operator, whose Sydney turnover it put above A0 million a week; it sought A00 million. The company argued a penalty above A00 million would render it insolvent, having A8 million in cash against more than A.1 billion in debt, and was rescued by a A00 million investment. Two former senior executives admitted breaches and were penalised; the Federal Court found two more had breached their duties in 2026.
entities.cite: Bell Review report, NSW Independent Liquor and Gaming Authority, September 2022; AUSTRAC Federal Court proceedings and penalty hearing, June 2025; ASIC proceedings against former executives, 2025-2026

entities.d: Macau's second-largest junket operator ran under-the-table betting alongside the licensed tables, on a scale prosecutors put in the billions. Its chairman was sentenced to 14 years in April 2023 for criminal association, illegal gambling and aggravated laundering; the fraud counts were overturned on appeal.
entities.cite: Court of First Instance, Macau SAR, April 2023; Court of Second Instance, January 2024

entities.d: Both properties entered non-prosecution agreements and forfeited $7.45 million over years of taking play from an illegal bookmaker whose income they had reason to question. A former MGM Grand president was separately convicted of failing to file the required report.
entities.cite: US Attorney, C.D. Cal., non-prosecution agreements January 2024; US v. Sibella, conviction 2024

entities.n: British Columbia casinos — the Cullen Commission
entities.role: Casino operators and the provincial regulator
entities.d: A public inquiry found that hockey bags of $20 notes were accepted at Lower Mainland casinos for years while regulators and government knew and did not act. The commissioner declined to call it wilful blindness by individuals and located the failure in the institutions instead.
entities.cite: Commission of Inquiry into Money Laundering in British Columbia, final report, June 2022

entities.d: The firm that replaced Mossack Fonseca as the region's largest incorporator appeared throughout the Pandora Papers, having formed thousands of structures whose beneficial owners it had not verified. It says it complied with the law in force at the time; no charge has been brought.
entities.cite: ICIJ Pandora Papers, October 2021

entities.d: Delaware, Wyoming and Nevada companies can be formed in minutes with no verified owner, and appear repeatedly in trafficking and laundering files. The Corporate Transparency Act was to end that from 2024; an interim rule in March 2025 exempted domestic companies from reporting, leaving the requirement on foreign entities only.
entities.cite: Corporate Transparency Act 2021; FinCEN interim final rule, March 2025

entities.role: Encrypted handset network — run by police
entities.d: After Phantom Secure closed, the FBI and Australian police built and distributed the replacement themselves, reading roughly 27 million messages from 12,000 devices before the takedown in June 2021. More than 800 arrests followed across 16 countries; the admissibility of the material has been litigated ever since.
entities.cite: US v. Iosif Florea et al., S.D. Cal., indictment June 2021; AFP Operation Ironside

entities.d: A platform sold with modified handsets and a remote wipe function, taken down in September 2024 with 51 arrests across Europe, Australia and North America. Its alleged administrator, who had run it from his parents' house in Sydney, was arrested there.
entities.cite: Europol and Eurojust coordinated action, September 2024; AFP charges

entities.d: Found on a phone belonging to a man convicted of murdering a Dutch crime journalist, and taken down in December 2024 after French and Dutch investigators monitored it for three months and read 2.3 million messages. It ran on more than 40 servers and admitted users by invitation only.
entities.cite: Europol and Eurojust, Operation Passionflower, December 2024

entities.d: Dutch and German police read the service for five months before closing it in February 2023, then raided a drug lab and two cocaine sites the messages had identified. Its operators were prosecuted in the Netherlands.
entities.cite: Dutch Politie and Europol action, February 2023; Netherlands prosecutions from 2023

entities.d: The first of the European encrypted-phone takedowns: 19,000 handsets, servers seized in Canada, and an owner convicted of laundering and weapons offences. The recovered message store has been used in Dutch murder and trafficking trials for years since.
entities.cite: Dutch Openbaar Ministerie prosecution from April 2016; Rotterdam District Court conviction

entities.n: Grupo Wisa and Balboa Bank & Trust
entities.role: Free-zone trading group and its bank
entities.d: A trading group in the Colon Free Zone, a duty-free retailer, a newspaper and a bank were designated together as a trade-based laundering network for several trafficking organisations. Panama's regulator seized the bank and wound it down; one of the designated principals later pleaded guilty in Miami to a bank-fraud conspiracy.
entities.cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designations, May 2016; Superintendencia de Bancos de Panama seizure, 2016

entities.d: An undercover investigation recorded intermediaries, one of them an ambassador-at-large, offering to wash cash through the state gold refinery and export it as bullion. Gold turns cash into a commodity with an invoice; the government appointed a commission and the practice continued.
entities.cite: Al Jazeera Investigative Unit, Gold Mafia, March 2023; Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe statements

entities.role: Container port and strait crossing — access control
entities.d: Spain's largest container port sits eight miles from Morocco, and the hashish and cocaine networks around it have recruited from the municipal police, the customs service and the port workforce. Successive operations there have arrested serving officers rather than only dockers.
entities.cite: Spanish Policia Nacional and Guardia Civil operations, 2018–2024; Audiencia Provincial de Cadiz proceedings

entities.n: EU port corruption — the EUDA and WCO review
entities.d: A joint review found more than 1,826 tonnes of drugs seized in or bound for EU ports between January 2019 and June 2024, 1,244 tonnes of it at the ports themselves and 82 percent of it cocaine, concentrated at Antwerp and Rotterdam. Its finding on the mechanism is the one the individual prosecutions show: the size of the average consignment implies significant penetration of EU ports by criminal networks, including the likely corruption of some port staff. The vulnerability is staff access, not screening technology. Antwerp alone seized 116 tonnes in 2023, a record.
entities.cite: European Union Drugs Agency and World Customs Organization joint report, 2025; Belgian customs figures, January 2024

entities.d: German police seized the market's servers in March 2024 and the US Treasury designated its administrator, an Iranian national, in a rare case of naming a market operator by name rather than only the platform. It had roughly 30,000 users and 1,000 vendors selling narcotics.
entities.cite: BKA seizure, March 2024; OFAC designation, March 2024

entities.d: Agreed to about $450 million in opioid settlements through bankruptcy, having marketed a reformulated oxycodone as harder to abuse than the evidence supported. New York had already obtained a separate settlement over the same claims.
entities.cite: In re Endo International plc, S.D.N.Y. bankruptcy, settlement 2022; New York State settlement 2021

entities.d: Settled a Nevada Gaming Control Board complaint for $10.5 million over hosting patrons with convictions for illegal bookmaking and money laundering, including one who had been barred from the state's casinos. Its president departed before the settlement was approved.
entities.cite: Nevada Gaming Commission settlement, 2025; Gaming Control Board complaint, 2024

entities.role: Licensed tuna companies and ten blocked vessels
entities.d: Fifteen Ecuador-based targets were designated on 20 August 2026 and ten fishing vessels identified as blocked property, over a network run out of Manta for Los Choneros and Los Lobos. The fleet does not carry the cocaine: it meets the go-fast boats at sea and supplies refuelling, food and medical assistance while watching for law enforcement, so a licensed vessel with a legitimate reason to be offshore becomes the service station for the crossing. Treasury noted the boats used government-subsidised fuel, which puts a state subsidy inside the cost structure of the route. One designated operator was said to coordinate 30 to 40 tonnes a month; another owned or controlled six companies, five of them in marine fishing. The Ecuadorian navy took 1.8 tonnes off a small fishing boat off Manabi in April 2026.
entities.cite: US Treasury press release sb0610 and OFAC designations under E.O. 14059 and E.O. 13224 as amended, 20 August 2026; Federal Register notice, 25 August 2026; Ecuadorian Ministry of National Defense seizure, 1 April 2026

entities.d: A Culiacan gas company designated with its owner, whose organisation Treasury says had laundered at least $16.5 million for Sinaloa Cartel clients including Los Chapitos and the Zambada faction. Fuel distribution moves cash volumes that would draw attention anywhere else.
entities.cite: OFAC designation under E.O. 14059, 2025

entities.d: Nine Guatemalan businesses have been designated across two actions as property of an organisation that controls trafficking on the Mexican border and supplies the Sinaloa Cartel. The companies are the part of the structure that survives a change of leadership, which is why Treasury relisted them.
entities.cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designations, December 2019; E.O. 14059 designations, February 2024

entities.n: Afghan hawala houses — the Barakzai network
entities.d: Two Kandahar exchange houses were designated with the opium network that used them, one belonging to the network's head and one to its main financial conduit. Hawala settles by ledger between brokers rather than by transfer, so there is no wire for a bank to screen and no correspondent to hold liable.
entities.cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designations, 2012; Afghan Threat Finance Cell investigation

entities.n: Afghan and UAE trading companies — the Mohammad Din network
entities.d: Four companies in Afghanistan and the UAE were designated as vehicles for a Helmand heroin operation running labs in Musa Qala and Sangin. Dubai's role in the Afghan opiate economy is where the proceeds are placed rather than where the drug moves.
entities.cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designations, 2014

entities.d: Treasury identified a facility in the coastal province run by a presidential cousin as producing 84 million captagon tablets in 2020, coordinated with the Fourth Division and Hezbollah contacts. Manufacture at that volume needs presses, precursor supply and export clearance, which is why the map treats it as industry rather than as a lab.
entities.cite: OFAC designation under E.O. 13582, March 2023

entities.d: The EU designated several private security companies as shells for pro-regime militias involved in the drug economy. The security licence is the cover: it explains armed men, vehicles and access to sites without any of it needing to be accounted for as military.
entities.cite: Council of the EU designations, April 2023

entities.n: The Joumaa exchange houses and used-car network
entities.role: Money exchange houses and vehicle trading
entities.d: Treasury designated a Lebanese-Colombian trafficker along with nine associates and 19 businesses, describing a system that moved as much as $200 million a month through exchange houses, bulk cash and used-car sales in the United States resold in West Africa. A Virginia indictment followed, charging the coordination of at least 85 tonnes of Colombian cocaine with Los Zetas. He has never been in US custody.
entities.cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, January 2011; US v. Joumaa, E.D. Va., indictment November 2011

entities.n: Operation Cedar — the luxury goods circuit
entities.d: Simultaneous raids in France, Belgium, Germany and Italy broke a laundering circuit that converted European cocaine proceeds into watches, cars and diamonds bought in Europe and resold in the Middle East. Goods carry value across borders without a wire transfer, which is the same mechanism the gold and used-car cases show.
entities.cite: DEA Operation Cedar, February 2016; French, Belgian, German and Italian prosecutions

entities.d: A Karachi-based exchange group designated by Treasury as laundering for drug organisations, designated terrorist groups and Chinese and Colombian networks at once, on an estimated multi-billion-dollar annual scale. Its principal was arrested in Panama, extradited, and pleaded guilty in the United States in 2016.
entities.cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, November 2015; US v. Khanani, D. Ariz., plea 2016

entities.n: Tri-border free zone trading — the Barakat network
entities.d: Argentina froze the assets of a Ciudad del Este trading network in 2018 and the US designated its principals; the free zone's paperwork lets goods, invoices and value move without matching cargo. It sits at the junction of the Paraguayan cocaine corridor and the region's largest informal remittance market.
entities.cite: OFAC designations 2004 and 2018; Argentine Unidad de Informacion Financiera freezing order, 2018

entities.n: The eight Wuhan and Hebei chemical companies
entities.role: Chemical manufacture and export — sales agents and payment handlers
entities.d: Eight China-based companies and eight employees were indicted in Florida in October 2024 over synthetic opioids and fentanyl precursors, with the charges naming who held each firm's bitcoin wallet or received its Western Union payments. Five of the companies have since ceased operating and China scheduled three of the chemicals involved, which had not been controlled when the sales were made.
entities.cite: US Department of Justice, M.D. Fla., indictments unsealed October 2024

entities.role: Chemical manufacture — director and senior staff
entities.d: A Wuhan company, its sole director and three senior employees were charged in Los Angeles with conspiring to manufacture and distribute fentanyl and with selling precursors and xylazine worldwide. The misbranded-drug counts alongside the trafficking counts are the tell: the same shipments were being described to customs as something else.
entities.cite: US v. Hubei Aoks Bio-Tech Co. Ltd., C.D. Cal., indictment November 2024

entities.d: An Indian company and senior executives were indicted after selling an undercover agent 25 kilograms of a listed fentanyl precursor twice, then negotiating four tonnes of it — half destined for Sinaloa, half for the United States — for about $380,000. It had advertised the chemicals openly on its website and at trade shows.
entities.cite: US Department of Justice and DEA, indictment announced March 2025

entities.n: Chinese precursor vendors and crypto payment
entities.d: Blockchain tracing puts inflows to Chinese precursor vendors at roughly $31 million in 2023, $35 million in 2024 and $39 million in 2025, with about 97 percent accepting cryptocurrency and most marketing xylazine or nitazenes alongside the precursors. A 2026 indictment of Shandong suppliers added a material-support-to-a-terrorist-organisation count, available because Mexican cartels were designated in February 2025.
entities.cite: US indictment of Shandong-based suppliers, 2026; TRM Labs blockchain analysis, 2026

entities.n: Law firm escrow accounts — the Ravenell case
entities.d: A prominent Baltimore defence lawyer was convicted after a 16-day trial of using his firm's escrow and operating accounts to move more than a million dollars in drug proceeds, pay counsel for other members of the conspiracy, and invest on a trafficker client's behalf. He was sentenced to 57 months. Escrow is the one account a lawyer can hold for a client without explaining whose money it is.
entities.cite: US v. Ravenell, D. Md., verdict December 2021, sentence June 2022

entities.role: Informal brokers — cash collection and mirror transfer
entities.d: Brokers who buy cartel cash in the United States at a discount and settle in China through mirror transfers have largely displaced the older Colombian peso exchange. Prosecutions in North Carolina, Georgia and Virginia have produced sentences of six to fifteen years and forfeitures in the tens of millions; the demand side is Chinese nationals needing dollars abroad, which is what makes the service cheap.
entities.cite: US Department of Justice, W.D.N.C. sentence 2026; E.D. Va. sentences 2024–2025; DEA National Drug Threat Assessment

entities.n: Sham technology company — the Bibliowicz case
entities.d: A senior executive was convicted by a Brooklyn jury of laundering more than $300 million for cartels including Sinaloa, routed behind a technology company that existed to explain the flows. He was sentenced to 12 years with a $330 million forfeiture judgment.
entities.cite: US v. Bibliowicz Mitrani, E.D.N.Y., verdict December 2025, sentence April 2026

entities.n: High-value freight forwarders — the jewellery corridor
entities.role: Specialist parcel carriers — jewellery and fine art
entities.d: An organisation working from a jewellery-store front in the Los Angeles Jewelry Mart shipped locked cases of cocaine to New York's Diamond District through forwarders that specialise in precious metals and fine art, and sent the cash back the same way. At least 1,300 parcels moved between the two cities. Carriers built for high-value goods offer sealed handling and few questions.
entities.cite: US v. Rodriguez, O'Connell and others, C.D. Cal., superseding indictment 2025

entities.role: Commercial road freight — brokers and drivers
entities.d: An Ontario investigation found a broker-style operation inside the licensed trucking sector, with drivers knowingly moving loads within legitimate supply chains; 21 people were charged with 104 offences and about 1.7 tonnes of drugs seized. Road freight has no equivalent of the port's fixed choke point, so the recruitment happens at the brokerage.
entities.cite: Windsor Police, CBSA and Ontario Provincial Police, Project Bay, 2025–2026

entities.n: Airport ground handling — the NAHCO case
entities.role: Cargo handling company — import shed manager
entities.d: A cargo manager at Nigeria's main aviation handling company pleaded guilty to stealing and trafficking 25 kilograms of ephedrine from the import shed inside the customs area at Lagos airport, and was sentenced to three years. Ground handling sits on the airside of every control and is rarely counted as part of the supply chain.
entities.cite: Federal High Court Lagos, NDLEA prosecution, conviction December 2025

entities.n: Sahel gold and real estate — laundering the cocaine surge
entities.role: Artisanal gold buyers and property developers
entities.d: Cocaine seizures across Burkina Faso, Chad, Mali, Mauritania and Niger rose from an average of 13 kilograms a year between 2015 and 2020 to 1,466 kilograms in 2022, and Mauritania alone took 2.3 tonnes by mid-2023. The UN found the proceeds moving into gold and real estate, sectors growing fast enough to absorb them, and named armed groups in Mali among the beneficiaries. No prosecution has followed in any of the five states.
entities.cite: UNODC, Drug Trafficking in the Sahel, April 2024

entities.n: Faria Lima funds and fintechs — Operation Carbono Oculto
entities.d: Brazilian authorities identified some 26 billion reais of PCC money laundered over four years through investment funds and fintechs in Sao Paulo's financial district, alongside a fuel scheme covering illegal methanol imports, over a thousand petrol stations, and a port terminal, ethanol plants and a truck fleet held inside more than 40 funds. Fintechs were not then regulated as financial institutions, which is what made the transactions hard to follow. Named firms deny wrongdoing and describe themselves as used rather than complicit.
entities.cite: Operacao Carbono Oculto, Receita Federal and Sao Paulo GAECO, from 28 August 2025

entities.role: Fuel importers, blenders and retail stations
entities.d: Methanol entered through the port of Paranagua on falsified paperwork, was diverted to blenders who mixed it into petrol, and reached consumers through stations the organisation controlled. Prosecutors put illicit fuel imports at 10 billion reais and retail sales at 52 billion. Buyers were defrauded twice over, on volume and on specification, which is the rare instance on this map where the laundering vehicle harms the public directly rather than only carrying the proceeds.
entities.cite: Operacao Carbono Oculto findings, Receita Federal and ANP, 2025

entities.n: The Shimada network and the leaked raid
entities.role: Payment and trading companies moving proceeds in crypto
entities.d: Two Brazilians, three Brazilian companies and one Portuguese company were designated on 1 July 2026 over a laundering network running between Florida and Sao Paulo. Treasury put the sum at more than $30 million generated in US cities and moved back to Brazil in cryptocurrency; the FBI had already arrested six of the Florida node in January 2026. One of the designated companies had surfaced a year earlier in a laundering network tied to a Sao Paulo football club whose agent was said to work for the PCC. What happened next is the record: Brazil's federal police had a parallel operation ready, and their chief said the uncoordinated US designation forced them to execute their warrants earlier than planned. The associate was captured; the principal escaped and is a fugitive.
entities.cite: US Treasury press release sb0549 and OFAC designations under E.O. 14059 and E.O. 13224 as amended, 1 July 2026; FBI arrests and indictment, S.D. Fla., January 2026; Brazilian Federal Police Operation Exchange and statements by the Federal Police director, July 2026

entities.role: Conglomerate — construction, mining, gems, fuel, retail
entities.d: Founded in 1998 with drug revenues under the privileges of a ceasefire deal, the group spread into construction, agriculture, gems and minerals, petroleum, electronics and department stores, with offices in Yangon, Mandalay and Lashio as well as Wa territory. Treasury designated 16 companies in 2005 and a further 17 with 26 individuals in 2008 as the commercial network of the United Wa State Army; US prosecutors sought $103 million in forfeitures tied to the group. It later traded under a different name and its founder remains a fugitive.
entities.cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designations, November 2005 and November 2008; US v. Wei Hsueh Kang and others, E.D.N.Y., indictment unsealed January 2005

entities.n: The Menu-Based Sanctions list — a head of state without an asset freeze
entities.role: Sanctions instrument rather than a firm
entities.d: Haiti's former president was placed on the Non-SDN Menu-Based Sanctions list rather than the main blocking list, which prohibits foreign-exchange transactions and bars US financial institutions from lending to him without freezing his property outright. The distinction matters for what a designation actually does: the graduated tier reaches banking relationships while leaving assets untouched, and it is the tier chosen for a designated former head of state.
entities.cite: OFAC Non-SDN Menu-Based Sanctions listing under E.O. 14059, August 2024

entities.d: Peru's state company holds the sole legal right to buy and sell coca leaf, registering around 31,000 producers and exporting to a US firm that extracts cocaine for medical use. Researchers examining the country's main legal coca valley found the monopoly pays below what traffickers offer, so most of the crop leaves the legal channel it was designed to capture. It is the one entry on this map where the state itself is the licensed buyer of the raw material.
entities.cite: Busnel and Manrique Lopez, International Journal on Drug Policy, 2023; ENACO producer registry

entities.role: Statutory regime — possession and transfer of drug benefits
entities.d: Thirty-two men were convicted in 2025 alone under the Confiscation of Benefits Act, which makes possessing or moving the proceeds of drug dealing a separate offence from trafficking. The largest single laundering sentence, 38 months within a 28-year term, concerned removing about S$1.27 million from the jurisdiction. The sums are small by the standards of every bank on this layer, and the sentences are not: the same conduct that draws a corporate fine elsewhere draws imprisonment and caning here.
entities.cite: Singapore Central Narcotics Bureau convictions, 2024 and 2025; Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act 1992

entities.d: More than 60 Indian suppliers exported roughly $130 million of tapentadol pills to West African countries that had not approved the drug, at doses above the Indian manufacturing cap. Regulators had seized one manufacturer's stock and halted production after an earlier investigation; exports of the same opioid then rose. A regulator's own reply named only two firms as approved to make tapentadol for export in 2019-2024, and neither appears among the 60. Around 30 percent of West Africa's population is estimated to use tramadol or codeine.
entities.cite: Bellingcat and Newslaundry investigation, April 2026; CDSCO records obtained under RTI; BBC Eye investigation, February 2025

entities.d: Treasury designated an Indian online pharmacy and two nationals who worked with Dominican and US traffickers to sell counterfeit pills marketed as discounted legitimate medication and filled instead with illicit fentanyl. The same online suppliers sell precursor chemicals to Mexican laboratories, so one channel serves both the finished counterfeit and the raw material for it.
entities.cite: OFAC designations, September 2025; DEA public warning, October 2024

entities.d: Treasury designated the casino and its owner's organisation in January 2018, stating it was used to store and distribute narcotics from Myanmar's United Wa State Army and to launder the proceeds, with drug seizures in Thailand, Laos and China traced back to it since 2014. The owner denied the allegations at a press conference within days. The casino kept operating and expanding, which is the clearest single measure on this map of what a designation is worth inside a jurisdiction that will not act on it.
entities.cite: OFAC Transnational Criminal Organizations designation, January 2018; subsequent UNODC reporting on the Golden Triangle SEZ

entities.d: UNODC counted more than 340 licensed and unlicensed casinos across the lower Mekong by early 2022, and describes them with online gambling and stablecoin transfers as a parallel banking system handling proceeds from drug trafficking, illegal gambling and cyberfraud. The displacement is documented: enforcement against Macau's junkets moved the business into Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and the Philippines, and operations there moved it again toward border and remote areas. Treasury designations in Cambodia have reached casino complexes and two banks connected to them.
entities.cite: UNODC, Casinos, Money Laundering, Underground Banking and Transnational Organized Crime in East and Southeast Asia, January 2024; OFAC designations in Cambodia, 2025-2026

entities.n: BVI and Dubai shells — the Gacanin structures
entities.role: Free zone company formation and local sponsorship
entities.d: Leaked corporate records showed a Bosnian trafficker designated by the US and by Europol partners had used British Virgin Islands and Dubai free zone companies to employ men prosecutors describe as his cartel's operatives. UAE law at the time required a local sponsor, and one was named on the filings; the sponsor's representative said she had no knowledge of narcotics or laundering. Bosnian prosecutors allege the same organisation paid politicians and worked with the head of the state security service.
entities.cite: ICIJ analysis of leaked corporate records, August 2024; OFAC and Europol-coordinated designations with the Netherlands, France and Belgium

entities.n: Operation BULUT and the afterlife of seized message stores
